Operation 1027, an anti-regime offensive launched by the Three Brotherhood Alliance on October 27, 2023, toppled the cross-border empires run by Kokang’s notorious “Big Four” families—the Bai, Wei, Ming and Liu clans. The alliance comprised the TNLA, MNDAA and Arakan Army. Parallel crackdowns were launched in areas controlled by the UWSA and NDAA. Yet far from marking the demise of the scam industry, the dismantling of those border scam complexes simply scattered the surviving networks, driving them deep into Shan State’s interior.

From the border to the interior

According to local residents, hundreds of Chinese nationals arrived in southern Shan State’s Laihka Township around November 2023, approximately a month after Operation 1027 began. Locals said the newcomers first erected compounds near Manpang Village before launching scam operations.

Instead of operating out of massive, conspicuous complexes housing huge numbers of people as they previously did, they rented homes dispersed throughout residential neighborhoods to fragment their workforce, and even set up makeshift tent encampments in rural villages and forests.

Starting in February 2026, the regime began conducting raids against online scam compounds in Laihka. According to official releases, as of the end of October, 129 Chinese nationals had been arrested, comprising the majority of those detained.

According to statements given by detainees, they crossed into Myanmar from Xishuangbanna, in the far south of China’s Yunnan Province, entering UWSA-controlled Panghsang and the NDAA-controlled Mong La area. From there, coordinated networks facilitated their phased, step-by-step relocation across northern, southern and eastern Shan State.

Similarly, in northern Shan, residents noted that telecom fraud operators began trickling into Tangyan town in early 2024.

According to UWSA statements, during crackdowns on scam operations in Tangyan in November 2024 and July 2025, Wa forces arrested over 1,000 people, 829 of whom were Chinese nationals.

The military junta likewise launched its own raids and arrests in Tangyan across 2024 and 2025.

Despite raids conducted by both the junta and the UWSA, a military sweep proved that these criminal syndicates were still operating in Tangyan in April 2026. During a raid on an online scam camp near Kaung San Village, the military reported arresting 123 individuals, 103 of whom were Chinese nationals.

“Local youths worked at the scam centers. Usually, whenever there’s a raid, those who can run simply flee. Some get away, some don’t. But we’ve never heard of the actual bosses being caught,” a Tangyan resident said.

Throughout 2025, these fraud networks spread rapidly into numerous townships in Shan State: Mongyai and Hsipaw in northern Shan; Nansang and Mongpan in southern Shan; and Kengtung and Mong Hsat in eastern Shan.

In October 2026, the regime announced the arrest of 75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar citizens involved in online scams in southern Shan State’s Hopong Township, along with the seizure of related equipment. This indicates that scam operations have spread to the doorstep of Taunggyi, the capital of Shan State.

Ko Michael, an analyst who tracks cyber-scam activities, said the crackdowns by both the regime and local armed groups have stalled because they consistently fail to net the masterminds.

“They aren’t shooting the birds; they’re just shaking the trees. So the birds simply fly from one tree to another. Everything gets scattered around. That’s why this problem has become so difficult to contain,” he said.

At the same time, while scam operations have proliferated into the interior, they have by no means vanished from the borderlands. None of the ethnic armed groups conducting anti-scam crackdowns have declared their regions entirely free of fraud hubs. Operations persist in the border town of Muse, and recruitment s seeking workers for scam centers in Tachileik on the Thai border continue to appear daily on social media. The fact that cyber-scam operations continue to operate on Shan State’s borders while simultaneously spreading inland raises a key question. Who is enabling this aggressive proliferation?

Who is providing protection?

The vast majority of individuals arrested in Shan State’s scam hubs are Chinese nationals; in some locations, nearly every person detained was from China. Yet it would be utterly impossible for foreign nationals to arrive in large groups and establish, let alone operate, these telecom fraud enterprises without local assistance.

Crucially, armed organizations and security outfits controlling the territory in these areas are the linchpins ensuring the survival of these organized crime syndicates. When cyber-scams first proliferated across the Kokang, Wa and Mong La borderlands, they took root strictly under the control of local armed actors.

In many parts of Shan State, regime-aligned armed factions have turned these operations into lucrative revenue streams, according to local residents and individuals formerly involved in the trade.

“The total proliferation of scams across Shan State didn’t happen because of just one group. But I want to stress this: it would be completely impossible to run without the military’s involvement,” said Ko Michael, the scam-operation monitor.

In December 2025, after the military raided an online scam compound in Hsipaw Township, state media reported the arrest of three members of the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), one of the major Shan armed groups. Concurrently, residents point out that in Muse, Laihka and several other areas, local militia outfits—including the Namhkam Myoma, Pansay, Kaungkha, Manpang and Wanpang militias—receive payoffs in exchange for facilitating relocations, providing physical security and protection, and transporting workers to scam centers.

“The scam business and armed groups are inseparable. Without an armed group, you simply cannot run a scam operation. It’s the armed groups that provide the protection,” said a resident of Muse.

The nexus between armed actors and telecom fraud extends to Myanmar’s most powerful ethnic armed organization, the UWSA, which has been heavily implicated in the scam industry despite its current anti-scam crackdowns.

“The ones who really laid the solid groundwork and operated these scam rings at scale were the Wa. Top Wa leaders were directly involved,” said Dr. Hla Kyaw Zaw, a veteran analyst of China-Myanmar affairs.

The Chinese state-produced documentary “The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar,” which covered the anti-scam crackdowns and was aired last month, identifies UWSA-controlled territory as the incubator for northern Myanmar’s scam economy. It claimed that Bao Yanban, chief of Mong Pawk, a town in the Wa region, amassed so much wealth from the scams that he would sun-dry banknotes on rooftops to prevent mold.

Protection for scam operators has come not only from local militias, but directly from the regime itself.

In late 2023, as the Three Brotherhood Alliance was attempting to capture Laukkai during Operation 1027, the military regime sheltered top Kokang scam kingpins from the Big Four families in Naypyitaw. Among them was Bai Suocheng, the former leader of the Kokang Self-Administered Zone and head of the regime-aligned Border Guard Force.

It was only under immense pressure from Beijing in January 2024 that the regime finally handed these high-profile suspects over to Chinese security forces in Naypyitaw. They were subsequently tried in Chinese courts, where harsh penalties—including death sentences—were handed down.

What is the impact?

Despite the crackdowns and legal cases, online scam syndicates have continued to fan out from the northern Shan-China border across the entirety of Shan State, causing severe social harm in every community they penetrate.

With legitimate employment opportunities devastated by the country’s ongoing military conflict, cyber-scam compounds have emerged as places where local youth can make quick money.

A northern Shan resident who previously worked in a scam compound explained that the prospect of “easy money” causes those who have worked in the industry to lose interest in conventional jobs.

“When you return from there [working at a scam center], you come back with a lot of money. You just don’t want to do outside manual work anymore. Once that money runs out, you don’t go looking for decent, ordinary jobs. That’s true for about 80 percent of the people who go to work there,” the northern Shan resident explained.

As the industry has expanded, training courses designed to teach people how to run telecom scams have begun popping up in Shan State, according to sources close to the industry.

“There are training courses opened by people who worked inside scam compounds. They teach combined computer and communication skills. They teach basic things like how to defraud people out of money. How many words per minute you need to type—that’s something only people who worked there can teach,” said a resident of Kyaukme in northern Shan State. Citing security concerns, the resident declined to disclose the exact locations or other details of the training centers.

Scam operations also serve as a seemingly safe and profitable haven for young people trying to escape military conscription by the regime. The conscription law, which has been on the books for years but only enforced since 2024, requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve up to two years in the military.

A Kyaukme resident who sought to evade conscription by working in a scam compound said he did so for his own safety. “My name came up on the conscription list. A lot of people from our area worked there. They said things were going well there, inviting us to come over,” he said.

“Quite a lot of young people ended up going,” he added.

World.title: Regime Summons German Envoy Over Call for Coup Releases
World.content:
YANGON—The Myanmar regime’s Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s top resident diplomat on Tuesday over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi.

Germany’s mission head Mathias Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the president of Aung San Suu Kyi’s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The junta behind the coup organized elections installing a nominally civilian government this spring, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

Licharz said in his message, scheduled for Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said Licharz was summoned for a meeting with deputy minister Ko Ko Kyaw, “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire.

“Should the Chargé d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” a statement said.

Myanmar has been riven by civil war since the 2021 coup, as pro-democracy guerrillas rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority insurgencies challenging central rule boiled over.

The ministry statement accused Licharz of “intentional conduct” that “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest.”

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” it said.

Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 coup, which ended Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions—charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet and he’s not allowed to communicate independently.”

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyitaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

Licharz called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained including U Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi.”

World.title: Myanmar Embassies Push Tax, Remittance Rules as Migrant Backlash Grows Across Asia
World.content:
Embassies operated by Myanmar’s cash-strapped military regime have intensified efforts to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, even as migrant opposition grows across Asia.

For the past two weeks, Myanmar missions have repeatedly ordered that all passport applications must be accompanied by official evidence of remittance and tax payments.

The regime enforced a mandatory 25 percent remittance requirement alongside 2 percent income tax on migrant workers in 2023 — measures widely seen as a bid to bolster foreign currency reserves amid severe shortages.

In the latest notices, Myanmar missions in Singapore, Hong Kong and Macau declared Monday that migrants applying for a Passport for Job (PJ) or PJ extension must include proof of tax payment and remittance of a quarter of their earnings over the past three months through official regime channels.

“The Myanmar embassy is issuing the order but nobody wants to use official remittance channels,” a 30-year-old Myanmar national working at a florist in Singapore told The Irrawaddy.

“Applicants may comply with the rule for three months, but otherwise, they will continue to use alternative channels that are convenient, pay more, and don’t siphon money to the military.”

He added that waiting times for passport extension appointments have also expanded dramatically under the regime’s new digital identification system (UID), prompting worker fears of being stranded in a legal limbo.

“A friend of mine has been waiting three months for an appointment; previously it took just two weeks to extend a passport.”

The precise number of Myanmar migrants in Singapore is unknown, but Myanmar labor department data from 2024 suggested a sharp increase since 2021, prompting predictions they could reach 200,000 in a few years.

Other major destinations for Myanmar migrant workers are South Korea and Japan, which recruit through formal MOU frameworks and offer comparatively higher wages.

Regime embassies in Seoul and Tokyo were among the first to double down, issuing notices that workers must comply with remittance and tax rules in exchange for passport extensions.

“It’s a new requirement. Even If workers have not used official channels before, they must do so before applying for an extension,” a South Korea-based Myanmar national who assists migrant workers told The Irrawaddy.

“Workers have no option if they need their passports extended. So, they have to comply for at least three months,” she said.

She echoed the complaints of long appointment waiting times, higher application costs, and workers’ reluctance to use official channels that offer lower exchange rates while funneling money to the military regime.

Meanwhile, the regime’s embassy in Thailand — home to the largest Myanmar migrant community of roughly four million — is reportedly demanding remittance and tax evidence before it issues or extends PJs. Agents say the embassy requires proof of payments, adding that appointment waiting times are unpredictable.

“The process is really complicated now. We have been told to submit remittance proof, even though they haven’t publicly announced it,” a Bangkok-based agent told The Irrawaddy.

The regime’s Certificate of Identity (CI) process to identify undocumented workers in Thailand was rejected by over 2 million migrants in a recent poll. Only 15,000 out of nearly 750,000 ID-less migrants have shown up at Thai CI centers amid a widespread boycott triggered by the tax and remittance rules.

Thailand’s Labor Ministry has voiced opposition to the rules, which it views as a violation of worker rights. However, regime Labor Minister Maung Myint pressed the issue on Sunday, insisting that CI applicants must abide by the remittance and tax mandates.

World.title: Kazakhstan Faces Economic Overheating Risks Despite Strong Growth, IMF Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s economy continues to grow faster than its sustainable potential, with domestic demand exceeding the economy’s capacity, Roberto Cardarelli, assistant director of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) Middle East and Central Asia Department, said at a presentation of the Fund’s regional economic outlook.

Cardarelli said signs of economic overheating persisted not only in Kazakhstan but also in Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic, where inflationary pressures remain elevated, Kazinform reported on Nov. 11.

He explained that potential economic growth represents the pace at which an economy can expand without generating additional inflationary pressure. When actual growth exceeds this level, demand can outstrip the economy’s ability to supply goods and services, contributing to rising prices.

“Of course, demand is there, and demand exceeds what the economy can sustain,” Cardarelli said, adding that Kazakhstan’s inflation performance compares favorably with that of many neighboring countries.

He also noted that regional governments are taking measures to ease overheating and bring economic growth closer to sustainable levels.

IMF outlook points to continued expansion

The comments come as the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) at $397.9 billion in 2026, rising to $553.4 billion by 2031.

The IMF forecasts real GDP growth of 4.4% this year, accelerating to 4.9% in 2027 before moderating to approximately 3.5-3.8% annually through 2031.

Nominal GDP per capita is projected to increase from $15,006 in 2025 to $19,311 in 2026 and $25,539 by 2031.

Inflation is expected to average 10.3% in 2026, compared with 11.4% in 2025, before gradually declining to 5% by 2031. The unemployment rate is forecast to decrease from 4.6% in 2025 to 4.3% by 2031.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev referred to the IMF’s economic projections in his recent state-of-the-nation address, noting that Kazakhstan is expected to rank among the world’s 50 largest economies by GDP.

Fiscal pressures and investment prospects

The IMF also projects an increase in government revenues and expenditures, with spending continuing to exceed income over the forecast period.

Government revenues are expected to reach 37.3 trillion tenge (US$82.7 billion) in 2026, while expenditures are projected at 39.3 trillion tenge (US$87.2 billion), resulting in a deficit of approximately 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion).

The deficit could widen to 5.7 trillion tenge (US$12.6 billion) by 2031.

Public debt is projected to increase from 45.9 trillion tenge (US$101.8 billion) in 2026 to 93.9 trillion tenge (US$208.3 billion) in 2031. Its share of GDP is expected to rise from 23.8% to approximately 29.8% over the same period.

Investment is forecast to account for 28.4% of GDP in 2026, increasing to 32.2% by 2031.

The current account balance is expected to return to a surplus of $2.2 billion in 2026, following a $12.5 billion deficit in 2025. However, the IMF projects a return to deficits from 2027, potentially reaching $16 billion by 2031.

The IMF released its October 2026 World Economic Outlook on Oct. 13. Its separate Regional Economic Outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia was published on Oct. 22.

World.title: Kazakhstan Increases Renewable Energy Generation More Than 16-Fold in Decade
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan increased electricity generation from renewable energy sources (RES), excluding large hydropower plants, more than 16-fold over the past decade, reaching 8.7 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025.

By the end of 2025, renewable energy accounted for 14.5% of the country’s total electricity generation, including large hydropower plants. Without large hydropower, the share stood at 7%, reported the Bureau of National Statistics on Nov. 11.

Including large hydropower plants, renewable electricity generation rose from 9.5 billion kilowatt-hours in 2015 to 17.9 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025. Their share of total electricity generation rose from 10.4% to 14.5%.

Meanwhile, the share of renewable energy excluding large hydropower plants grew from 0.6% in 2015 to 7% in 2025. Generation from these sources increased from 536.5 million to 8.69 billion kilowatt-hours over the same period.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks Third Globally in Land Restoration Efforts, Covering 8.13 Million Hectares
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranks third worldwide in the area of land covered by restoration efforts, with 8.13 million hectares, or approximately 3% of its territory, included in such initiatives, according to the first global Nature’s Comeback report published by United Nations agencies.

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the UN Environment Program (UNEP), and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity prepared the report. China ranks first with 127.4 million hectares, followed by Mongolia with 12.18 million hectares, reported the Agriculture Ministry on Nov. 12.

Digital monitoring and soil protection

Alongside restoration initiatives, Kazakhstan is expanding efforts to monitor soil conditions, identify degraded agricultural land and improve the sustainable management of its land resources.

In 2025-2026, digital land degradation maps covered 114 million hectares. Surveys identified 2.7 million hectares of degraded agricultural land, providing data to prioritize areas for targeted restoration and soil protection measures.

A key step in strengthening the country’s regulatory framework was adopting the Law on Soil Protection on July 8. The legislation establishes legal mechanisms for soil assessment, protection and restoration.

The Agriculture Ministry and local executive authorities are also developing regional soil protection plans. These will include measures to prevent land degradation, restore agricultural areas and preserve soil productivity.

Kazakhstan’s approach combines ecosystem restoration with digital monitoring, stronger legislation and regional planning, focusing on protecting soil fertility and maintaining the long-term productivity of its land resources.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Build Settlement for 33,000 Near Balkhash Nuclear Power Plant
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to transform the village of Ulken on the shore of Lake Balkhash into a modern settlement for up to 33,000 residents as part of preparations for the country’s nuclear power plant projects.

The development will include housing, schools, healthcare facilities, vocational training centers and business infrastructure, Chairman of the Atomic Energy Agency Almasadam Satkaliyev said during a Nov. 12 meeting with Kazakh specialists working at Türkiye’s Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant.

Satkaliyev stressed that the project would not create an isolated workers’ settlement but would involve the comprehensive development of the existing village, according to the agency.

“This will not be a separate workers’ settlement. It will be the development of Ulken with all the supporting infrastructure necessary for living,” he said.

The plans include residential buildings, educational and medical facilities, training and retraining centers, hotels, service businesses and opportunities for entrepreneurship. Infrastructure initially built to support nuclear power plant construction could also be repurposed for the village after construction is completed.

Ulken is also expected to incorporate modern digital solutions and develop its tourism and recreational potential, leveraging its location and natural landscape along Lake Balkhash.

Workforce and training

According to Satkaliyev, construction of one nuclear power plant could require up to 15,000 workers at its peak, including civil engineers, welders, installers, electricians and automation and quality control specialists.

Once operational, each plant would employ approximately 2,000 people, including nuclear engineers, reactor operators and specialists in nuclear and radiation safety, maintenance and equipment repair.

To meet these requirements, Kazakhstan plans to establish a training center in Ulken and expand cooperation with domestic universities and specialized educational institutions in China and Russia.

Kazakh citizens will also have opportunities to pursue postgraduate studies and professional internships abroad through the Bolashak international scholarship program, which provides dedicated quotas for nuclear industry training.

Satkaliyev said developing Ulken would create new jobs and career opportunities, particularly for young people and added that specialists recruited for the projects would be provided housing.

Kazakhstan draws on Akkuyu experience

The announcement followed Satkaliyev’s visit to the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant construction site in Türkiye, where a Kazakh delegation reviewed construction progress, engineering operations and preparations for future plant personnel.

Representatives of Akkuyu Nuclear, led by CEO Sergey Butskikh, briefed the delegation on the four reactor units. According to the company, the first unit’s main systems have reached an advanced stage of readiness for commissioning operations. Hydraulic tests of the reactor’s primary and secondary circuits have been completed, while the second unit has had its main reactor equipment installed and welding on the main circulation pipeline completed.

Key reactor components have also been installed at the third unit, while construction and assembly work continues at the fourth. The four units are scheduled to enter operation at one-year intervals.

The delegation also visited the first unit’s control facilities, the coastal pumping station and the training center, where it reviewed the system for preparing operational personnel.

Kazakhstan seeks to build its nuclear industry

During a separate meeting with Kazakh citizens employed at Akkuyu, Satkaliyev invited them to bring their professional experience and expertise to Kazakhstan’s emerging nuclear energy sector.

He said experience gained through participation in a major international project would be valuable for both the construction and operation of nuclear power plants in Kazakhstan.

The country is working to establish a broader nuclear industry cluster encompassing uranium production, scientific research and the development of specialized expertise. Its strategy also envisages building at least three nuclear power plants.

Satkaliyev noted that plans for the first two projects in the Lake Balkhash area had become more defined, while Kazakhstan was expanding cooperation with international partners, including Russia, China, Hungary and South Korea, to strengthen workforce training and technical expertise.

The Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant, under construction in Türkiye’s Mersin Province on the Mediterranean coast, is the country’s first nuclear power plant. Developed by Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, the project comprises four VVER-1200 reactors with a combined planned capacity of 4,800 megawatts. Kazakh specialists working at the facility are gaining experience that could contribute to Kazakhstan’s nuclear energy sector.

World.title: Kazakhstan and Germany Advance Energy Cooperation, Explore Green Hydrogen Projects
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Germany are exploring new opportunities in renewable energy, green hydrogen and carbon capture technologies as the two countries seek to expand industrial and technological cooperation. Representatives of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy and Joachim Bertele, deputy director of the Asia-Pacific Department at Germany’s Federal Foreign Office, discussed the energy agenda on Nov. 11.

The talks covered cooperation in the oil and gas sector, conventional energy, renewable energy sources and green hydrogen, the ministry’s press service reported.

Kazakhstan presented renewable energy projects being implemented with German companies Goldbeck Solar GmbH and Solarnet Investment GmbH. Both sides highlighted the importance of advanced technologies and knowledge exchange to support the energy transition.

Green hydrogen was another key focus. Kazakhstan outlined its cooperation with German research institutions and technology companies, including the Reiner Lemoine Institut, which researches hydrogen energy, water resource data digitalization and expert knowledge exchange.

The two sides are also discussing potential cooperation with Linde on carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies.

The meeting also addressed the Hydrogen Diplomacy Office in Astana, operating with support from the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ). Germany reaffirmed its interest in developing hydrogen cooperation, recognizing Kazakhstan’s potential to produce and use green hydrogen and the need to support the required technologies and infrastructure.

Separately, Kazakhstan and Germany held political consultations at Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, led by Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issagaliyev and Bertele.

The discussions focused on implementing agreements reached during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Germany on Sept. 29-30.

The delegations also reviewed the 2026-2028 Joint Roadmap for Industrial, Technological and Raw Materials Cooperation and discussed opportunities in critical raw materials, transport and logistics, digitalization and advanced technologies.

Education, research and cultural ties were also on the agenda, alongside cooperation within the Central Asia-Germany format and engagement with the European Union and international organizations.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to expanding bilateral ties ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027.

World.title: Central Asia Needs Institutions That Work Between Summits
World.content:
The C6 has rebuilt political trust since 2018. Turning more than 200 regional initiatives into results now depends on permanent bodies with clear mandates.

When the leaders of Central Asia and Azerbaijan met in Avaza, Turkmenistan, on Oct. 8, it was the first Consultative Meeting of Heads of State with Azerbaijan as a full participant. The wider format links Central Asia with the South Caucasus and, through it, with European markets.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev used the summit to raise a practical question. He noted that more than 200 initiatives have been put forward since 2018, while only a small share has been implemented, and proposed that the foreign ministries take inventory of them. The proposal leads to a broader question about how the region can deliver on its commitments without permanent institutions to carry them out.

Uzbekistan’s opening in 2016 started the return of regional trust

After the Soviet collapse, the five republics inherited integrated production chains and a common infrastructure network. Over the following decades, closed borders and unresolved territorial disputes pulled them apart. The Ferghana Valley, the region’s most densely populated area, suffered most from border restrictions and periodic violent clashes.

Change began in 2016, when President Shavkat Mirziyoyev opened Uzbekistan’s economy and borders. The Consultative Meetings, launched in Astana in 2018, then became the main platform for rebuilding confidence among the region’s leaders. Russia’s war in Ukraine and growing uncertainty over northern trade routes later raised interest in southern and trans-Caspian connectivity.

Border settlements have opened the Ferghana Valley to cooperation

On March 13, 2025, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon signed a border treaty after armed clashes in 2021 and 2022. On March 31, the presidents of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan met in Khujand. They signed a treaty fixing the junction point of their three borders, along with the Khujand Declaration of Eternal Friendship.

The second Ferghana Peace Forum, held in Guliston, Tajikistan, on Sept. 28-29, brought together the governors of the three border provinces. A valley once known for border conflict is becoming a space for cross-border trade and joint development.

Trade and travel data show the gains of renewed trust

In November 2025, Mirziyoyev reported that intraregional trade had doubled over eight years to about $11 billion and that mutual investment had grown 5.6 times. Uzbekistan’s trade with its neighbors tripled from $2.4 billion in 2016 to $7.2 billion in 2024, and the number of joint enterprises passed 1,800.

Travel recovered as well. In the first nine months of 2017, about 379,000 Uzbek citizens traveled to Kyrgyzstan. In the same period of 2018, the number rose to 2.42 million. In 2025, foreign visits to Uzbekistan to see relatives reached 7.86 million.

Joint investment is also growing. Under the agreed structure for the Kambarata-1 hydropower plant, Kyrgyzstan holds 34%, while Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan hold 33% each. The three countries held the third round of talks on an intergovernmental agreement for the project in Almaty in September 2026. Much of this progress still rests on political leadership and bilateral deals.

Institutional integration lags behind political rapprochement

A company working in several Central Asian markets often needs separate registration and certification in each. Trade and transit rules remain fragmented, partly because Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic belong to the Eurasian Economic Union while their neighbors do not. The region also lacks a common framework for recognizing professional qualifications, which limits the benefits of growing labor mobility.

Water and energy management is the most pressing case. Upstream hydropower and downstream irrigation require coordinated planning, especially as climate change reduces water availability, yet cooperation still depends on bilateral negotiations. Newer areas such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity raise the same coordination problem. Azerbaijan’s participation adds trans-Caspian opportunities and makes regulatory interoperability more important.

More than 200 initiatives need a body responsible for implementation

Mirziyoyev addressed the same concern in Avaza. He called for “a flexible and transparent format in which strong, sovereign, and independent states cooperate.” He also said that implementation matters more than the number of documents, and made clear that Tashkent does not want heavy new structures.

The two positions describe a real dilemma. The region needs stronger mechanisms to deliver agreed priorities, while governments remain cautious about bodies that could constrain sovereignty. Institutionalization need not mean a supranational government. The practical question is whether the C6 states will delegate narrowly defined coordination and monitoring functions to joint bodies. Without them, responsibility stays spread across national ministries, and initiatives lose momentum once leaders return home.

Other regions show that integration can coexist with sovereignty

Under Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union, the EU acts only within the competences member states have conferred on it. Its institutions set common market rules, while national authority remains intact outside the agreed mandates.

ASEAN offers a model closer to Central Asian preferences. It rests on consensus, yet the ASEAN Secretariat’s Integration Monitoring Directorate tracks compliance with agreed economic measures in support of the ASEAN Economic Community Council. In MERCOSUR, the 1994 Ouro Preto Protocol established intergovernmental bodies, including a Trade Commission that monitors the common trade policy.

None of these models is flawless. The EU struggles with complex governance, while ASEAN and MERCOSUR have faced implementation gaps and recurring trade disputes. All of them rely on institutions that work between summits and turn political decisions into action.

A permanent architecture would complement the Consultative Meetings

The heads of state should remain the highest platform for setting priorities, while implementation passes to regional bodies with clear mandates.

A C6 Regional Coordination Secretariat could operate under the rotating chairmanship with a small permanent staff that keeps a registry of commitments and publishes annual progress reports. A permanent team would prevent the loss of institutional memory at each rotation. Specialized councils on water and energy, customs, transport and digital policy would bring national ministries and regulators together.

Over time, and subject to national approval, governments could delegate limited regulatory functions in selected areas, starting with mutual recognition of qualifications and cross-border transport procedures. Full customs harmonization would remain a long-term goal given Eurasian Economic Union commitments.

Every major C6 declaration should come with an action plan naming responsible institutions and deadlines. A public online dashboard could show businesses and citizens what regional cooperation delivers. These bodies should be judged by whether they lower transaction costs and improve the management of shared resources.

Shared institutions can strengthen the sovereignty of smaller states

Governments can keep final authority over the scope of cooperation and delegate specific functions through clear agreements with consensus decision-making and parliamentary oversight. No single country can manage transboundary rivers and transport corridors, so joint institutions would increase each member’s effective capacity. A C6 framework would also help the region engage the EU, China, Russia, the United States and Türkiye while preserving independent foreign policies.

The next summit could adopt an institutional reform agenda

Tokayev’s call to review existing initiatives could be the starting point. The review should go beyond sorting relevant commitments from outdated ones. The C6 countries could commission a joint assessment of current mechanisms and a phased roadmap toward permanent coordination bodies, which the next summit could adopt in place of a new list of declarations.

The transition will be gradual, and differences among the six economies call for flexibility. The region has built political trust over the past decade. Its next task is to build institutions that work between summits.

The author is Sobir Kurbanov, an economist at Nightingale Int., a geopolitical intelligence and advisory firm focused on Central Asia and Greater Eurasia.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan Signs $1.2 Billion in Energy Agreements at COP31
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has signed agreements worth approximately $1.2 billion to develop renewable energy and modernize gas infrastructure during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

The agreements provide for the construction of wind power plants with capacities of 150 megawatts in the Turkistan Region and one gigawatt in the Kostanai Region. They also cover the Aqyl Energy project, which involves installing 1.35 million smart gas meters with remote data transmission. They also signed additional documents to expand international cooperation on environmental protection.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov attended the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Framework Convention on Climate Change on the instruction of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. In his address, he outlined Kazakhstan’s environmental priorities, including reforestation, water security and the transition to cleaner energy, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Nov. 11.

Bektenov said the Taza Qazaqstan initiative had evolved into a nationwide movement, with more than six million people participating in environmental activities. Over the past five years, the country has planted nearly 1.7 billion trees, with another 270 million seedlings planned for 2027. This would bring Kazakhstan closer to its target of planting two billion trees.

He also called for stronger international cooperation on water security, highlighting Tokayev’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the UN’s auspices.

“Addressing environmental challenges requires closer cooperation,” Bektenov said, referring to the Regional Ecological Summit held in Astana in April. The summit resulted in the adoption of the Declaration on Environmental Solidarity of Central Asia, providing a framework for regional cooperation.

Kazakhstan is also expanding its renewable energy capacity. The share of renewables in the country’s energy mix quadrupled over the past six years, reaching 8% this year. The government aims to increase it to 15% by 2030.

Other priorities include nuclear energy, wind and solar power, green hydrogen production, and a joint Green Energy Corridor project with Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan to facilitate clean electricity exports.

Bektenov also highlighted Alatau City as a prospective low-carbon urban development project and Kazakhstan’s use of artificial intelligence and satellite monitoring to forecast natural hazards and improve emergency prevention.

At the national pavilion, Kazakhstan presented projects focused on reforestation, methane emission reduction, waste recycling and industrial decarbonization. The exhibition also featured initiatives to restore the Northern Aral Sea, protect the Caspian ecosystem and develop a green energy corridor across the Caspian Sea to Europe.

The pavilion showcased digital solutions, including a regional AI-powered carbon platform, satellite-based climate monitoring and the proposed Caspian Climate Shield adaptation system.

On Nov. 10, Kazakhstan launched its Just Energy Transition Investment Platform (QaJET) at COP31 in Antalya, with the EBRD offering up to $100 million in concessional financing and grants and up to $1 billion in potential direct financing.

World.title: Kazakhstan Tests Tokenized Government Securities in First National Bank Issuance
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has taken its first practical step toward introducing tokenized securities into its capital market, with the National Bank placing 10 billion tenge (US$2.2 million) worth of digital short-term notes on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE). The issuance marks a transition from establishing the legal framework for digital financial assets to testing how they can function within the country’s existing financial infrastructure.

The auction took place on Nov. 9, with the same issue offered simultaneously in traditional and tokenized forms. The National Bank offered the full 50 billion tenge (US$110.9 million), including 10 billion tenge in tokenized notes. The securities have a maturity of 91 days and a weighted average annual yield of 15.72%.

Investor demand reached 70.2 billion tenge (US$155.7 million), exceeding the offering by 1.4 times, the bank reported.

The parallel placement allowed the National Bank to test the new technology while maintaining identical pricing conditions for both forms of the instrument.

How tokenized notes work

Tokenized notes are financial instruments issued in digital form, with investors’ ownership rights recorded through a digital platform. The National Bank remains the issuer and is responsible for fulfilling its obligations to investors.

KASE provides the infrastructure for issuing, placing and circulating the notes. KASE records ownership rights on its digital financial assets platform and reflects them in the Central Securities Depository’s registry, while the KASE Clearing Center handles clearing and settlement.

This arrangement integrates digital technology with established financial market institutions rather than replacing the existing system.

What it means for the market

The main potential benefit of tokenization is making capital markets more accessible and efficient. Digital platforms can facilitate the issuance and transfer of financial instruments, automate certain operations and potentially reduce transaction costs.

For businesses, this could create additional channels for raising capital. For investors, it could expand the range of available instruments and potentially lower entry barriers through fractional ownership.

However, these benefits will depend on market adoption, investor demand, liquidity and the reliability of the regulatory and technological infrastructure.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov, commenting on the development in his Tengenomika channel publication, described the issuance as an important step in moving Kazakhstan from building the regulatory and technological foundations for tokenization to its practical application.

From regulation to implementation

Kazakhstan’s legislative framework for issuing and circulating digital financial assets took effect on May 1. KASE became the country’s first registered operator of a digital financial assets platform and trading platform.

National Bank Chairman Timur Suleimenov said the next priority was to expand the infrastructure’s practical use, attract new issuers and broaden the range of digital financial instruments.

KASE is also prepared to assist potential issuers with structuring transactions, onboarding and preparing securities for placement.

The first issuance demonstrates that tokenized instruments can operate within Kazakhstan’s existing financial market infrastructure. The next test will be whether businesses and other market participants adopt the technology more broadly, turning an initial transaction into a functioning segment of the domestic capital market.

World.title: Who runs Poland? Why the president and the government cannot agree
World.content:
Political crisis in Poland



A sharp political crisis has erupted in Poland. The president and the government are accusing each other of violating the Constitution, while the opposition is speaking of a coup. What is happening in a country that has become one of the main immigration hubs in Central Europe, and should foreigners be worried about their future there?

What happened in Warsaw

On October 30, police appeared outside the building of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal. Judges elected by the parliamentary majority but not sworn in by President Karol Nawrocki attempted to take up their duties. One of them, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, announced the removal of the tribunal’s president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy.

The tribunal’s leadership refused to recognise the legality of what was happening. Opposition supporters gathered outside the building, and a standoff with police began.

President Nawrocki, who was on his way to Senegal for an official visit, turned his plane around and returned to Warsaw. He went to the tribunal building and accused the government of attempting to seize control of a state institution.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk, by contrast, said the government intended to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal could operate independently and lawfully.

The events of October 30–31 were reported by Reuters and Euroradio.

The word “coup” has once again entered Poland’s political debate. But is this really an attempt to seize power?

“If we are to say that a coup took place on Friday, then we must also say that it began back in 2015, when the struggle over the Constitutional Tribunal started to move beyond legal boundaries,” says Michał Potocki, a political commentator for the Polish newspaper Dziennik Gazeta Prawna, in an interview with Euroradio.

In his view, the events of October 30 are simply the latest episode in a conflict that has been going on for eleven years.

Why politicians are fighting for control of the constitutional tribunal

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal reviews whether laws comply with the Constitution. Its rulings can constrain the actions of parliament and the government, making control over the institution politically significant.

The current crisis began in 2015, when the conservative Law and Justice party (PiS) came to power. Its judicial reforms sparked protests at home and a confrontation with the European Union. European institutions accused the Polish authorities of undermining judicial independence.

In 2023, a coalition led by Donald Tusk took office. It pledged to restore the independence of the courts and reverse controversial decisions made by its predecessors. But delivering on those promises proved difficult: initially, its initiatives were blocked by President Andrzej Duda and, since 2025, by Karol Nawrocki, who is politically aligned with PiS.

As a result, different branches of government are challenging the legality of one another’s actions.

“At its core, this is a struggle for control of the Constitutional Tribunal, which can either help the government or obstruct its legislative agenda,” Potocki says.

The expert, however, does not consider either side beyond reproach.

“Both sides have violated the Constitution. Law and Justice did so more often and to a greater extent. But, unfortunately, the Civic Coalition has its own share of wrongdoing,” he notes.

Polish legal experts have also raised questions about the methods used by Tusk’s government. As The Guardian reports, constitutional law specialists are divided over the legality of the decision to remove the tribunal’s president. Some critics of PiS also consider the legal grounds for the move questionable.

Could the crisis paralyse the state?

Despite the dramatic events in Warsaw, Poland is not yet facing a breakdown of its system of government.

According to Potocki, the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively been unable to function normally for about two years. Nevertheless, the country’s other state institutions continue to operate.

The danger lies elsewhere: prolonged confrontation is eroding public trust in the courts, politicians and the state itself.

The Constitutional Tribunal is supposed to act as an independent arbiter, resolving disputes over the legality of government actions. But when judges and politicians themselves challenge one another’s authority, that mechanism ceases to function.

Potocki notes that some Polish political forces are calling for a complete overhaul of the tribunal and the appointment of a new panel of judges through compromise. So far, however, no agreement has been reached.

That is why the current conflict matters not only to Polish politicians but also to the millions of people who live in the country and depend on decisions made by its public institutions.

What the political crisis means for migrants

In recent years, Poland has become one of the main immigration destinations in Central Europe. Hundreds of thousands of foreigners live and work there, including people from Ukraine, Belarus, Georgia and other countries. They include migrant workers, students, people who have moved for family reasons, and refugees who cannot safely return to their home countries.

To varying degrees, all of them depend on Polish state institutions: they apply for residence and work permits, renew their documents and seek international protection. A prolonged conflict between branches of government is therefore bound to cause concern.

However, the political crisis does not mean that migration services will stop operating or that foreigners will automatically lose their right to reside in Poland.

“This will have no direct impact, because the Constitutional Tribunal does not deal with the legalisation of residence, Pole’s Cards or other issues faced by citizens of Belarus and other countries,” Michał Potocki explains in an interview with Euroradio.

At the same time, Poland’s migration system was already under considerable strain before the current crisis.

As Euroradio reported, Olga Dobrovolska, a lawyer at the Belarusian Solidarity Centre, said that more than 190,000 applications for legalisation of foreigners’ residence were awaiting consideration in the Mazovian Voivodeship alone. The situation is also particularly difficult in the Lower Silesian and Pomeranian Voivodeships. The introduction of the MOS electronic application system has so far failed to reduce the queues.

For refugees, these difficulties are compounded by the question of international protection. According to Dobrovolska, Polish authorities assess applications individually, examining whether a person would face danger if they returned to their home country. References to political events from previous years alone may not be sufficient.

There is no direct link between these problems and the events surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal. But, as Potocki points out, a constitutional oversight body that is not functioning properly limits the opportunities to seek systemic solutions to problems involving violations of rights.

The expert cites lengthy delays in processing residence applications as an example. When statutory deadlines are not met, a properly functioning Constitutional Tribunal could potentially examine whether such practices comply with constitutional guarantees.

When the legitimacy of the tribunal itself is being contested, however, it becomes much harder to use this mechanism.

The main risk for migrants, therefore, is not the immediate loss of their documents or legal status, but the weakening of the legal safeguards intended to protect their interests in dealings with the state.

Who benefits from the conflict?

The political crisis in Poland is being actively exploited by Russian and Belarusian state propaganda.

As Euroradio reported, the events surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal have provided an opportunity to claim that a coup is supposedly taking place in the country.

According to Potocki, the propaganda campaign has several objectives. Above all, it seeks to portray Poland as a country engulfed in chaos and undermine public trust in democratic institutions.

Belarusian propaganda is also using the conflict to challenge Poland’s right to criticise violations of democracy in Belarus.

Another objective is to deepen divisions between Poland’s political camps, including by exploiting disagreements over Ukraine and relations with the European Union.

However, Potocki stresses that the Polish government and the president remain broadly aligned on fundamental issues concerning Russia and the need to support Ukraine. Their differences are primarily about political approaches and individual decisions.

What happens next?

Experts do not expect the crisis to be resolved quickly.

Parliamentary elections are due to take place in Poland in 2027. The confrontation between the ruling coalition and PiS is already becoming part of the election campaign, leaving politicians with fewer and fewer incentives to compromise.

“Unfortunately, I do not see much chance of a compromise. Polarisation in Poland will only intensify,” Potocki predicts.

For foreigners living in Poland, this means, above all, keeping an eye on government and parliamentary decisions that directly determine the rules governing residence, employment and state assistance.

For now, there are no grounds to claim that the conflict surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal threatens migrants’ right to remain in the country.

But Poland’s crisis illustrates a broader problem: even in a democratic state, political confrontation can weaken institutions for a prolonged period, undermining the mechanisms that protect human rights. For migrants, particularly refugees whose status often depends heavily on decisions made by the authorities, this has very practical implications.

World.title: Singer fined over song. What other forms of dissent can be punished in Georgia
World.content:
Singer in Georgia fined over song

Georgian singer Sofо Batilashvili has been fined 3,000 lari (about $1,150) for posting a video on social media of herself performing the song “Ole Ola”, which contains profanity directed at the ruling party. The ruling was issued by Judge Koba Chagunava.

After the hearing, Batilashvili told journalists that restrictions on forms of protest were becoming increasingly widespread in Georgia and that the issue had now extended to censorship of music.

“A year ago, it would have seemed absurd to arrest people for standing on the pavement. But now, in Georgia, we have reached a point where people are arrested for almost anything if they express resistance, take part in protests or show solidarity with protesters.

“We have reached a point where we could be handed a list of songs. They have already started drawing up lists of songs that cannot be performed. We are now dealing with censorship of musicians,” the singer said.

What happened

The song “Ole Ola”, which contains profanity directed at the ruling Georgian Dream party, has become an unofficial anthem of mass pro-European protests that have continued in Tbilisi for more than two years.

The protests began after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced on November 28, 2024, that Georgia, which has EU candidate status, would put its EU accession process on hold until 2028.

Sopho Batilashvili is not the first person to face punishment for performing the song in public.

On October 7, activist Tornike Toshkhua and student Sandro Sekhniashvili were summoned to court over performing “Ole Ola” in the street.

Batilashvili posted her video on October 8.

In her accompanying post, she said she objected to people being summoned to court over a song and was posting the video in protest, at 10 p.m. – the time when participants in the pro-European protests sing “Ole Ola” at rallies.

“People are being prosecuted in Georgia in 2026 over this song – I repeat, over a song. And I, who got tired of ‘Ole Ola’ a long time ago and have not even felt like humming it for years, suddenly decided: here you go,” Batilashvili wrote.

In her post, she also expressed solidarity with Georgian musician Kordz, the author of “Ole Ola”, who has openly opposed the authorities and faced attacks and threats from municipal officials, members of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media.

Kordz, whose real name is Aleksandre Kordzaia, has reported twice that attempts had been made to attack him.

As a result, the Kamara music festival in the town of Gori, where Kordz was due to perform, had to be postponed indefinitely in September. The organiser, the Danish Cultural Institute, said it considered it unsafe to hold the event.

In her Facebook post, Batilashvili stressed the importance of society refusing to accept such treatment of people.

“I know that many things have become normalised. I also know how people turn against you if you speak out. But we must remind ourselves that treating people this way is not normal, and that we still have each other’s backs. Otherwise, there is simply no point,” she wrote.

Unprecedented case

The fine imposed on Sopho Batilashvili may be considered an unprecedented case in Georgia.

One notable international parallel is Russia. In 2025, members of the band Stoptime were arrested in St Petersburg for performing songs by musicians critical of the Ukrainian and Russian authorities in public.

The band’s lead singer, Diana Loginova, known as Naoko, was fined on charges of “discrediting the Russian armed forces”, while the musicians were placed in administrative detention several times.

From social media to pavements: Georgia’s crackdown on protests

Since late 2024, the government led by Georgian Dream has tightened administrative and criminal legislation several times. As a result, people have faced penalties both for taking part in protests and for criticising government officials on social media.

● In February 2025, parliament added a new provision, Article 173, Part 16, to the Code of Administrative Offences. It defines verbal insults, abusive language and offensive behaviour towards state and political officials, civil servants and people holding equivalent positions as administrative offences.

The penalties range from a fine of 1,500 lari (about $600) to 4,000 lari (about $1,500), or administrative detention for up to 45 days.

The provision was soon used against people who posted statements and comments on Facebook criticising the government. In 2026, monitoring of social media posts became even more active.

● According to Human Rights Watch, a special unit set up within the interior ministry had referred around 300 cases of alleged administrative offences to the courts by August 2026.

● The legislative crackdown also extended to street protests. Amendments adopted in October 2025 increased penalties for obstructing roads and banned protesters from covering their faces. In some cases, fines were replaced with administrative detention, while repeat offences became subject to criminal prosecution.

● Further amendments adopted on December 12, 2025, extended restrictions to pavements and pedestrian areas. Under the new rules, organisers must notify the interior ministry in advance if an assembly or demonstration obstructs pedestrian movement.

Police were given broad powers to demand that protesters change the location or route of a gathering. Failure to comply can result in administrative detention of up to 15 days for participants and up to 20 days for organisers. Repeat violations may lead to criminal prosecution.

After the amendments came into force, police began detaining people standing on pavements and treating them as participants in protest rallies.

● Human rights organisations say the legislative changes disproportionately restrict freedom of assembly and expression and have become a tool for punishing peaceful protesters.

Human Rights Watch’s 2026 World Report also says that the human rights situation in Georgia has deteriorated sharply and that the government is using administrative and criminal measures to suppress critical voices.

World.title: ‘The ball is in Armenia’s court’: Yerevan voices on Armenia losing its voting rights in Russia-led CSTO
World.content:
CSTO strips Armenia of its voting rights

The Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) has stripped Armenia of its voting rights. The country has also officially lost the right to appoint representatives to key positions, a right it had effectively stopped exercising long ago. The CSTO member states’ leaders made these decisions on 11 November at a meeting of the Collective Security Council. Armenia’s prime minister did not attend.

The CSTO officially has six member states: Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia. Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO in February 2024. The country no longer takes part in the organisation’s activities or pays membership fees. Yerevan made the decision because the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations under its charter. The organisation did not respond when Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021–2022, despite the Armenian authorities’ appeals for help. The CSTO allies explained their inaction by saying it was “impossible” to confirm the incursions because Armenia and Azerbaijan had not delimited their border. Armenia’s prime minister responded: “If we say there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan, then there is no CSTO. The CSTO has an area of responsibility defined by borders. If there is no border, there is no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, there is no organisation.”

Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the leaders had taken into account Armenia’s failure to meet its obligations for several years. He was referring in particular to the country’s unpaid membership fees.

Under the organisation’s charter, Armenia can regain its rights in the CSTO once it clears its outstanding debt.

Yerevan has not yet officially responded to the CSTO’s decision. Perhaps the Armenian authorities saw no need to repeat their position, which they have stated many times before. A week ago, during a press briefing, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said, among other things: “I want us to make this clear once and for all: our interest in the CSTO has been exhausted.”

But Security Secretary Alen Simonyan had commented on the decision by the time this article went to publication. On his personal Facebook page, he wrote: “They stripped us of our voice in a place where everyone remained very loudly silent while they were collectively killing us.”

The CSTO member states’ leaders did not surprise experts or the public with their decision. Moreover, they believe Yerevan should not have waited for the organisation to strip it of its voting rights. Many argue that Armenia should have left the CSTO long ago.

Babken Harutyunyan, a politician and former member of the Hayrenik (Homeland) party, described the CSTO as a “pro-Azerbaijani organisation”. He explained his view by saying that Armenia’s allies treat their own member state and Azerbaijan, which they call a “friendly country”, as equals.

“The organisation is leaving the final step [leaving the CSTO] and the last word to Armenia itself. Or perhaps it hopes that forces it finds acceptable [pro-Russian forces] will come to power and once again bring Armenia back under the CSTO’s feet. After Azerbaijan’s years-long occupation of Jermuk and other Armenian territories, Armenia should leave the CSTO,” he said.

Пустующее кресло предназначалось для премьер-министра Армении

CSTO secretary-general: ‘Armenia’s expulsion from the organisation was not on the agenda at the Moscow summit’

CSTO Secretary-General Taalatbek Masadykov stressed that the organisation had not discussed expelling Armenia.

“For the past three years, Armenia has not paid its membership fees or sent staff to the CSTO Secretariat or the CSTO Joint Staff. In other words, although Armenia has formally remained a member, […] it has not taken part in discussions. If Armenia pays its membership fees, it will be able to regain its voting rights in the organisation. The decision is up to the Armenian leadership.”

Masadykov had previously said that Armenia had effectively already left the organisation:

“They listen to weekly reports, but do not take part in our main events, exercises and so on. So I think Article 25 [of the CSTO Charter] applies here. Essentially, they have already left of their own accord.”

Under Article 25 of the CSTO Charter, a member state loses its voting rights if it fails to pay its contributions or fill positions allocated to it under the organisation’s quotas.

‘A sign of deepening political and diplomatic tensions’

Vahan Babayan, chairman of the Reformist Party, said the CSTO’s decision to strip Yerevan of its voting rights was not merely a “technical or financial matter”.

“This is another sign of deepening political and diplomatic tensions between Armenia and the CSTO.”

He believes such decisions have the following implications:

“Armenia is losing its ability to influence the organisation’s decision-making process;

distrust between Armenia and Russia is growing in security and political matters.”

Babayan also warned that Armenia’s institutional standing within the organisation was weakening, even though the country formally remains a member of the military bloc. The politician said he expected the authorities to go beyond statements and provide serious, considered assessments in the interests of national security:

“We need real security guarantees, clear alliance relations and a foreign policy guided by national interests.”

Social media reactions

“Since the CSTO was founded, Armenia has been the only country that dared to speak up — and that is why it was stripped of its voting rights. Just like in an ancient Greek tragedy: you don’t know whether to laugh or cry.”

“They are still hoping that ‘Samvel from Kaluga’ [Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is under arrest and heads the opposition Strong Armenia party] or someone like him will come to power. Then they will restore Armenia’s voting rights. Otherwise, they would have kicked it out long ago.”

“Armenia should have left these stupid organisations, the CSTO and the Eurasian Economic Union [a Russia-led economic bloc], a long time ago. The only guarantee of Armenia’s security in the future is membership of the European Union and NATO.”

“Armenia decided to leave on its own. Nobody stripped it of any rights. Don’t delude yourselves.”

“And we didn’t need the right to vote anyway. They helped us in our time of need, and now they are taking away our rights? How hard this will be to bear. They don’t even recognise our state border.”

“And what even is the CSTO? A useless, unnecessary Putin-run organisation [a play on the Armenian abbreviation for the CSTO, ՀԱՊԿ, using different Armenian words]? The pointless ‘Putin office’ demands membership fees from Armenia but turned a blind eye to Azerbaijan’s invasion.”

“We have been stripped of our voting rights in a dead organisation.”

“Is it even worth worrying? What has this treacherous organisation ever done apart from betray us?”

“Thank God! I can’t wait for the day when Armenia has nothing in common with this rotten remnant of the Soviet Union.”
