World.title: Hegseth gives top award to soldier who scolded him at war cemetery
World.content:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to a service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery earlier this week.

Mr Hegseth posted photos to social media that show him pinning the award and shaking hands with the soldier.

His post says: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."

Pete Hegseth awards Specialist Thomas Iglesias after the serviceman reprimanded him. (X: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth)

Mr Hegseth welcomed the army unit that guards the tomb and gave Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026", the Pentagon said.

Specialist Iglesias reprimanded Mr Hegseth and a group of his staffers when a loud laugh was heard after they took photos at the site, following a ceremony that included US President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.

Video of the incident showed Mr Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

Pete Hegseth was at Arlington National Cemetery for a Veterans Day event. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

The tomb is considered one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the US, being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War.

It has been guarded around the clock, rain or shine, by a soldier from the US Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as The Old Guard, since 1948.

The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered one of the higher awards in the military and is not typically issued to junior enlisted service members.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said soon after a video of the reprimand emerged that the soldier "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum".

Pete Hegseth was attending a Veterans Day memorial event with Donald Trump. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

Scolding comes days after impeachment attempt

The scolding drew attention once more to the embattled defense secretary, who survived an impeachment attempt the day before.

The impeachment effort was led by Republican congressman Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.

While Mr Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed a bid to impeach him.

Inside Pete Hegseth's church The ABC visits US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's church, whose leaders challenge the legitimacy of democracy and key principles in the US constitution.

With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Mr Hegseth rebuked the move on Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the constitution for his removal, and framing the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

AP

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues impacting the tech giant's apps read our blog.

Microsoft said users could have trouble connecting to several of its Microsoft 365 services, including Exchange Online, Teams and SharePoint.

"We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online," a Microsoft spokesperson told the ABC.

Online outage reporting service Downdetector Australia recorded more than 4,400 reports of problems with Outlook by 8:20am today.

Australia's National Cyber Security Coordinator Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness is looking into it the outage. (ABC News: Peter Drought)

A spokesperson for the home affairs minister said the national cyber security coordinator, Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, was aware of the outage and was looking into it.

An update from Microsoft said some servers had become unresponsive and may involve a component that was supposed to check whether their services were healthy.

It said the company was investigating recent configuration changes as possible contributors to the problem.

Some Microsoft users said the Outlook problems was also restricting access to other services because they were unable to utilise two-factor authentication codes to log in.

Growing reliance on cloud service providers an issue

University of Melbourne associate professor Adel Toosi said the widespread disruption was the downside of a growing reliance on a handful of major cloud service providers.

Widespread Microsoft outage A global outage has hit Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

Dr Toosi said centralising services by using cloud computing providers such as Microsoft was often cheaper because of the economies of scale, but it also meant there was less redundancy if an error occurred.

While major providers typically distribute data across multiple geographical locations, Dr Toosi said they were still vulnerable to underlying flaws in the company's systems.

"If all of them are failing, nothing can be done," he said.

More than 120,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector have reported problems accessing Outlook. (Mike Mozart/Flickr.com/CC-BY-2.0)

Microsoft said it had tested an alternative way to check the health of some affected servers, allowing those machines to return to service.

It was applying the change more broadly and preparing an automated process to detect and restart servers that had stopped responding.

In an update issued at 8:41am AEDT, the company said it was continuing to restart and check affected servers before returning them to service.

World.title: Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients needing specialist care
World.content:
Residents and medical professionals say Western Australia's increasing reliance on fly-in,fly-out doctors for specialist care leaves country patients heavily exposed to skyrocketing regional airfares.

An interim report from the Productivity Commission released this week found regional Australians are paying excessive fares to travel within their own state.

The commission found short regional flights were on average 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major routes.

The same flights, often only provided by one operator, are used by medical specialists to visit regional areas across WA.

Latrice Porter manages a specialist medical centre in Albany. (ABC News" Will Corbett)

Specialist Centre practice manager Latrice Porter said airfare costs were a growing issue for regional practices.

She said locking in visiting staff for her centre in Albany, 400km south of Perth, was becoming increasingly more difficult.

"Rising airfare costs, limited flight availability, ongoing airline delays and cancellations are significantly increasing the cost of providing specialist outpatient care (in regional WA)," she said.

"The disruptions require clinics to be reorganised, accommodation arrangements amended and patients' schedules adjusted.

" It places more strain on already stretched healthcare resources. "

While remote healthcare such as telehealth is an option, Ms Porter said it is not fit for an "aging population".

Latrice Porter says the tyranny of distance makes it hard to find staff willing to travel to regional areas. (ABC News" Will Corbett)

"When we do provide telehealth services, we have a nurse sit in with the patient. It does take one of our staff members out of action," she said.

She believes that if costs keep rising, specialists servicing regional communities will have to start passing the cost of their travel onto patients.

Medical costs a burden on regions

While flights for regional residents are capped under a scheme subsidised by the state government, WA's Patient Assisted Travel Scheme (PATS) provides one of the lowest fuel and accommodation rebates in the country.

The burden is felt particularly heavily in the Pilbara, where Karratha woman Kim Simpson has been a long-time advocate for cheaper flights.

She said the expensive fares placed an unfair burden on regional patients seeking treatment.

Kim Simpson has advocated for cheaper flights. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

"I've got to go have skin cancers cut off my nose, Mohs surgery; they don't do that in Karratha so I've got to go down to Perth," she said.

"If it's something that you could have done in Karratha, but you don't want to wait, then PATS isn't going to cover that, so you've got to cover that fare yourself."

The impact of high airfares on families is also something Ms Simpson sees in the north-west.

"Lots of babies get born in Karratha, and then you want the grandies to come up, and that's going to cost them well over $2,000," she said.

FIFO traffic ensures Karratha Airport is WA's busiest outside Perth. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

With FIFO mining traffic making Karratha Airport WA's busiest outside Perth, Ms Simpson believes airlines feel they can get away with gouging mining communities.

"We don't all work for mining companies, and it's not fair that they treat everybody as if they're on huge dollars because there are a lot of people in the regions that are not," she said.

Loading...

" We get treated like second-class citizens, but we're paying first-class prices. "

The Productivity Commission's report found a lack of competition and high operating costs combined to push up airfares.

A final report is due in April next year.

World.title: Despite a 1960 doomsday prediction, the world won't end today
World.content:
According to a prediction three scientists made in 1960, the world was due to end today.

This "doomsday" was supposed to come not with a bang or a whimper, but from too many people.

The scientists had calculated that on Friday, November 13, 2026, the world's population would grow so quickly as to be near infinite.

"Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve to death," they wrote in a paper published in the journal Science at the time.

" They will be squeezed to death. "

Luckily, this prophecy has not come to pass.

Instead, in many countries, population decline is seen as a more serious concern than population growth.

So why was this doomsday warning wrong, and why is it still so difficult to predict population change?

How to calculate the end of the world

The paper's authors created a mathematical formula based on fertility rates and death rates and applied it to population estimates in the previous 2,000 years.

Their formula was on a "hyperbolic curve": It showed a world population growing at increasingly fast rates. Less and less time was needed for the population to double or triple.

Eventually, the formula predicted the world's population would shoot up to infinity at a single moment in time.

University of California Santa Barbara economist Javier Birchenall said there was an element of humour to the study.

The calculated end of the world happened to be the birthday of the paper's lead author, Heinz von Foerster, a researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign's department of electrical engineering.

"I don't think they were completely serious. They were trying to make a point that this is exceptional," Dr Birchenall said.

Loading...

Dr Birchenall highlighted the mistaken prediction in a paper in the same journal last month.

He initially did not want his paper to be published until November 13.

" My concern was, 'What if the world ends and these guys end up being right?' "

Despite being heavily criticised by social scientists at the time, the predictions were correct to a point.

"The numbers they produced made sense up until the 1980s," Dr Birchenall said.

But in the past four decades, the world's population has grown much more gently than the formula predicted.

In fact, the rate of world population growth reached its zenith just a few years after the doomsday prophecy, peaking at about 2.3 per cent in 1963.

The problem with predicting population

Dr Birchenall said the failed prediction demonstrated the risks of trying to treat a social pattern — population change — like a universal law.

"There's a difference between the way social systems respond and physical systems respond," he said.

University of Melbourne demographer Peter McDonald agreed.

"It is not possible to predict fertility with any degree of accuracy beyond about 10 years into the future," Professor McDonald said.

In 1960, the world had about 3 billion people. (Supplied: City of Coffs Harbour)

Past trends can be a good indicator of fertility rates in the short term, but in the longer term, they are going to respond to social forces that do not exist yet.

"The post-war baby boom which occurred in almost all advanced countries was not predicted by any of the leading demographers at the time," Professor McDonald said.

Population growth and resource risk

The doomsday prediction came amid fears about overpopulation in the 20th century.

Some countries responded to the threat with intense measures, such as China's One Child Policy.

Professor McDonald said overpopulation remained a big concern in some poorer countries with high fertility rates, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The African country's population is projected to double in the next 30 years, according to the United Nations, which could outpace its food resources.

"A failure of the harvest would have a devastating impact," Professor McDonald said.

The UN's current forecast sees the world population reaching its peak at just more than 10 billion in about 60 years, before slowly declining.

While population growth is not accelerating on a global scale, resource use still is. A 2024 UN report cautioned that the world's resource extraction was rising dramatically, driven largely by wealthier countries.

Reverse catastrophe unlikely

Dr Birchenall said fears had "flipped" in many places, with fertility rates falling below the rate of replacement.

One statistic spells challenge for Australia as it ages Australia is getting much older, and it is getting older faster than previously thought.

This has also driven warnings of cataclysm, and sparked the pronatalist movement, whose advocates claim falling birth rates are an existential threat.

Billionaire Elon Musk has said Australians are "disappearing", quoting a post on X that calls Australia's fertility rate a "catastrophe".

"Catastrophe is certainly the wrong word to use in Australia," Professor McDonald said, adding that Australia's fertility rate was "misleading" because of the number of temporary residents and immigration rates.

But he said there were some countries, particularly in East Asia, where low fertility rates and low migration were causing problems with aging populations.

"Massive increases in productivity would be required to offset this aging, but in the long term, the population disappears," Professor McDonald said.

Australia's immigration rate means it faces a lower risk from an aging population than some other countries. (Unsplash: Jay Wennington)

Dr Birchenall said while shrinking populations were an "important concern", they were equally unlikely to cause a global doomsday.

"But it's funny that it's the opposite of what people had in mind back in the 60s," he said.

" We all think that the world is ending in my generation. "

World.title: 30 years ago, the Spice Girls were global superstars. Now they swap parenting advice on a group chat
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCelebrity life 30 years ago, the Spice Girls were global superstars. Now they swap parenting advice on a group chat Gyan Yankovich November 13, 2026 — 10:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If they weren’t one of the most famous girl groups in the world, the Spice Girls could almost be confused for any other female friendship group who met, and tightly bonded together for life, in their 20s. “Sporty Spice” Melanie C was 22 when the band’s debut single Wannabe was released, parachuting the group – which also included Victoria Beckham, Geri Halliwell, Emma Bunton and Mel B – into the global spotlight. Now 52, and promoting her Melanie C World Tour, visiting Australia this week, Melanie says the group’s friendships have only gotten better with age. Melanie C is performing in Sydney on Sunday. The Spice Girls – Posh, Baby, Scary, Ginger and Sporty – pictured in 1997. “The lovely thing now is – because we’re older – we’re just so much more relaxed and respectful of each other. I think, you know, when you’re maybe in your 20s and even into the 30s, there was a bit more infighting because we get frustrated with each other,” she says on the Good Weekend Talks podcast.



“But now it’s like a lot of peace and everyone’s mums, and I’m waiting for the first Spice Grandma to be honest – and it’s definitely going to be Victoria [Beckham], isn’t it?” 30 years ago, the Spice Girls changed the world of pop. Instagram In a conversation with Courtney Thompson on the Good Weekend Talks podcast, Melanie confirmed the group have not one, but “a few” group chats – different ones for different things. And while she remains closest to Bunton, Melanie – who has one daughter, 17-year-old Scarlett – says some of the best parenting advice she’s ever received came from Halliwell. “Geri said to me, ‘When Scarlett’s a teenager, she will need you even more than she needs you when she’s a toddler’. And I was thinking, ‘No way, your babies need you, right? Your babies need you’ [but] oh my gosh, she was so right.”



Melanie “Mel C” Chisholm with her Australian husband Chris Dingwall. Getty Images Listen to the full episode, where Melanie C reflects on the pressure she faced during the height of Spice mania, why she feels more confident in her own skin in her 50s than ever before, and the joy of getting behind the DJ decks. Now in her 50s and entering a new phase of her life and career, Melanie has been reflecting on the person she was when she rose to fame with the Spice Girls, and who she is today. She says the two versions of herself really aren’t that different.



Editor's pick Good Weekend Mel C met her future husband on a celebrity dating app. She reckons she hit the jackpot “We get really bombarded with who we should be, you know, what everybody’s expectation of us are, and I think it can just it can just wobble your core,” she says. “And the thing for me – which, you know, really changed everything – is literally realising I didn’t have to look outside myself to be who I am. It’s all very much rooted and there. “And I think that’s what’s so important about people who’ve known you since you were a kid, you know, family, the friends you grew up with at school ... Get them to remind you that you’re brilliant. “Who you were when you were 10 years old, is who you are when you’re 50 years old.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer, alleged double murderer’s cross-examination continues; grilled by Crown over texts to Jesse Baird
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial. The accused has returned to the witness box today for further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. There is no dispute that the men died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol on February 19, 2024, and that the accused disposed of the bodies on February 22, 2024.

Former NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, right, has denied murdering Luke Davies and Jesse Baird, whose bodies were found in Bungonia, near Goulburn. Instagram; Bungonia; Facebook

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon planned to kill Baird after developing an obsessive and jealous infatuation with him and that he killed Davies, Baird’s boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence. The 31-year-old has told the court he had his police pistol with him because he had contemplated taking his own life the previous night over work-related trauma.

This is the accused’s recent evidence:

He denied that he was referring to harming or killing Baird when he texted the former TV presenter on November 18, 2023: “You don’t need to worry about seeing me out etc because you won’t exist and no further conversation needs to take place.” Baird had broken up with him on November 16. The accused told the court that he was referring to acknowledging him only.

Lamarre-Condon said that it was partly true when he claimed he had cancer in a message he sent to Baird from his friend’s Instagram account later in November. A naturopathic doctor in Bondi Junction had told him at the end of October or early November 2023 that a lump on his shoulder appeared to be “a form of sporadic cancer”, he said.

He said the doctor recommended he get a biopsy. “I did not follow through with the biopsy,” he said. He said he did alternative therapies that he had sourced online.

He admitted to throwing Baird’s phone off a bridge to destroy potentially incriminating evidence after he died.

The accused also admitted to “gaslighting” Baird when he denied that he had posted an Instagram story on November 9, 2023, that falsely implied Baird had sent him flowers. He said he later admitted the truth. Lamarre-Condon told the court that he limited the audience for the story one person, namely, a man that Baird had been seeing at this time.

He rejected a suggestion by the prosecutor that his “unrequited love [for Baird] turned into an obsession”.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: I made my own mistake in 1981, and the shame is rarely about the act alone
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion I made my own mistake in 1981, and the shame is rarely about the act alone Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain November 13, 2026 — 10:09am

November 13, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve thought about Newlands more than I expected to. Not the footage, which we’ve all seen, but the feeling that came with it. It was heavy and familiar, the sense that Australian cricket had been walking towards something like this for a while, and that a lot of us had watched it happen and kept quiet. Trevor Chappell sends down his infamous underarm delivery to Brian McKechnie. Channel Nine I’m not writing as a bystander. I made my own mistake in 1981, and I’ve lived with it long enough to know the shame is rarely about the act alone. It’s about knowing you had the chance to be better but inexplicably slipped up. That’s what I saw in the faces of those young men at Newlands. Three young men, one terrible decision



Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for 12 months and Cameron Bancroft for nine. Smith and Warner were barred from leadership roles. They broke the rules and they knew it. Nobody should pretend otherwise, and none of them has. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images But I could never watch that press conference and see only wrongdoing. I saw a captain who couldn’t hold himself together and a young opener who looked like he wished the floor would swallow him. These weren’t hardened cheats. They were young men who’d picked up on what the surrounding environment rewarded, and they did something they deeply regret and will carry for the rest of their lives. Others from the 2018 squad can say for themselves what they knew. Some may remember it differently, and that’s their right.



The culture we built Simon Longstaff’s review found Cricket Australia and the national team had drifted into a culture where winning mattered more than almost anything. I read that and felt implicated. I was part of that world for most of my life, as a player, captain, coach and commentator. Test captain Pat Cummins addresses the media on Friday in an attempt to put the 2018 sandpaper scandal behind him. Getty Images We told ourselves that hard, fair cricket was Australian cricket. We admired the stare and the sledge and the refusal to give an inch, and we mistook ruthlessness for strength. Nobody sat down and decided to build a culture that would produce Newlands. It crept in. A decision defended because it worked. A line crossed and forgotten because the team won. A young player watching what the senior men let slide and what they cheered.



I wish more of us had said, much earlier, that this wasn’t who we wanted to be. Hard cricket and honest cricket aren’t opposites. The best Australian sides I saw were fiercely competitive and still respected the contest. Somewhere along the way we lost sight of that. What a single afternoon costs I know a bit about being defined by one decision. The underarm still comes up at dinners, in interviews, in letters from strangers, more than 45 years on. Loading I’m not after sympathy. I made the call and it was mine to own. But it’s shown me how long one moment can follow a person, and how little room people leave you to be more than the worst thing you’ve done.



Another perspective Exclusive

Ball tampering ‘You can’t say sandpaper’: Coach allegedly told Smith, Bancroft to lie That’s partly why the aftermath of Newlands sat so badly with me. There was a fair argument that the bans were too harsh, and a fair argument that they weren’t harsh enough for men wearing the baggy green. I could see both. What troubled me was the appetite. At times, it felt less like a demand for accountability and more like a hunger to watch someone fall. Smith rebuilt his career through hard work and humility. Bancroft has spoken honestly about what it did to him. Warner spent years asking for his leadership ban to be reviewed. None of them escaped the consequences, and none should have. But a game that talks so much about character ought to be able to hold two ideas at once: what happened was wrong, and people can earn their way back.



Dave Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft during the 2019 Ashes in England. Getty Images I have empathy and admiration for Usman Khawaja, for confronting this head on. That he’s done it after eight years doesn’t make it any less significant or any less true. And the suggestion that he’s doing it to sell a book? Anyone who says that either doesn’t know the publishing industry or doesn’t know Uzzy. Uzzy isn’t making it up. The lesson that’s easy to miss



Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, is published by Penguin Random House and available from November 10. It’s tempting to say Newlands was the fault of three men, and the game is cleaner today for having punished them. I don’t believe that. The harder lesson points back at the rest of us. Everyone at Newlands knew the rules. What failed was whatever sits underneath them, the instinct that tells you what you will and won’t do when nobody’s stopping you and winning is on the line. That instinct is learned. It’s taught by example, in dressing rooms and boardrooms, by what we reward and what we let slide. What I’d say to a young player now



I meet young people in cricket for whom one bad decision, or a run of bad luck, can mean losing everything. I tell them what I wish someone had told me: you’ll be tested on a day when you’re tired and under pressure, surrounded by people who want the same result you do. Knowing the rules won’t be enough that day. You’ll have to ask yourself what kind of person you want to be. I didn’t always ask. Those three young men didn’t ask at Newlands. And the culture, which I helped build, never taught them to. Cricket will always ask its players to compete with everything they’ve got. I’d only add that how you compete matters as much as whether you win. We learned that slowly, and at a cost. I hope we don’t have to learn it again. There has been enough said now about Newlands. Let us not disinter its bones.

World.title: Masked thieves raid Chris Hemsworth Byron Bay mansion
World.content:
CultureCelebrityChris Hemsworth Masked thieves raid Chris Hemsworth Byron Bay mansion Nell Geraets November 13, 2026 — 10:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian actor Chris Hemsworth’s Byron Bay home was broken into on Wednesday morning, and the thieves stole three vehicles from the property. Police were called to the Hollywood star’s Broken Head home, south of Byron Bay, about 7.30am following reports of a vehicle theft. According to a statement from NSW Police, officers attached to the Tweed-Byron Police District attended the scene, and were told four unknown people had entered the property and stolen three vehicles. No injuries were reported. Chris Hemsworth and wife Elsa Pataky in New York in 2024. AP “Police established a crime scene and commenced investigations into the circumstances surrounding the incident. Two of the vehicles were later recovered,” police said in a statement. According to a 7NEWS report, Hemsworth’s wife, Spanish actor and model Elsa Pataky, woke to the sound of dogs barking about 2am on Wednesday. She ignored the noise.



However, when she checked their property’s CCTV cameras later that morning, she reportedly saw four men wearing balaclavas and two of them holding knives. Hemsworth called police shortly after. The four men had reportedly scaled the front fence, gaining access to a garage where the three cars were parked with their keys inside, 7NEWS reported. The couple’s home in Broken Head, near Byron Bay. The stolen vehicles are reportedly a BYD, a Ram and a Ford Raptor ute, the report said. One of the vehicles was recovered at Coraki, which is about an hour’s drive away from Hemsworth’s home, and another at Tabulam, which is more than a two-hour’s drive away. “On Thursday, police recovered a third vehicle in Lennox Head. All of the cars have been seized for forensic examination, and inquiries are ongoing. Anyone with information is urged to contact the police.”



Related Article Wine & spirits ‘A defining moment’: Can Chris Hemsworth put Australian whisky on the world map? There have been no arrests and no charges. The Thor actor has lived in the Byron Bay area with his wife for more than a decade, having moved back to his homeland from Los Angeles in 2014. Their luxury property, often described as “Fortress Hemsworth”, looks out over Seven Mile Beach and is reportedly worth around $50 million. Speaking on the SmartLess podcast in February, Hemsworth explained why he chose to relocate his family – which includes his three children – back to Australia. “It was right around the time my boys were born, and we kind of were set up in LA and not enjoying it,” he said. “Nothing was shooting there, we were filming kind of everywhere else.”



He also spoke of disliking the constant media attention and paparazzi associated with living in Los Angeles as a celebrity. Moving back to Australia had been the “greatest decision”, he said. Chris Hemsworth most recently starred as a jewel thief alongside Mark Ruffalo in Crime 101. AP “You know when you come back from work you want to go on a holiday? Coming home for me feels like a holiday … We have a big farm and horses and motorbikes and surf.” Hemsworth’s most recent film was Crime 101, Amazon MGM’s crime thriller in which the 43-year-old played a jewel thief. He will reprise his role as Thor in Avengers: Doomsday in December. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: ‘Khawaja is 100 per cent wrong’: Pat Cummins responds to sandpaper revelations
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Khawaja is 100 per cent wrong’: Pat Cummins responds to sandpaper revelations Jack Gramenz, Frances Howe and Tom Decent November 13, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australia’s Test cricket captain Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja is “100 per cent wrong” to say bowlers knew sandpaper was being used to rough up the ball during matches on the tour of South Africa in 2018. Former Test batsman Khawaja this week alleged “all of us” knew sandpaper was being used to rough up the ball during the 2018 tour, despite several players, notably the bowlers, having denied this in one of the biggest scandals in Australian cricketing history. Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins during an appearance on Friday. Sam Mooy Cummins said on Friday he’s taken his time “trying to understand exactly what” Khawaja has alleged, saying some of his claims are “probably true” “But I think there’s a few big leaps here, where he’s being vague … the details really matter,” he said.



“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100 per cent wrong. “I did not know that was happening.” Media prepare ahead of Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins appearance at Cricket Central in Sydney. Sam Mooy “[Khawaja] says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.” Cummins said he supported Khawaja’s “right to tell a story” and described Khawaja as a friend.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Khawaja cancels book interviews after refusing to answer key question about Cummins “But friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations.” When Cameron Bancroft was captured on camera putting a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 Test in Cape Town, Cummins was 24, playing his 13th Test “in a team that at that stage I think had a win at all cost mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there was too many silos within the team,” Cummins said. “Traits that I hope that everyone’s seen, and I tried very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain.” Following Khawaja’s claims, a key figure involved in a player review after the scandal subsequently called on Cricket Australia to reopen an investigation into the use of sandpaper in 2018.



David Warner, vice-captain at the time and one of three players suspended over the incident, described Khawaja’s version of events as 100 per cent accurate. Interest in the scandal’s resurgence this week has only grown as the days went on. The media turnout for Cummins on Friday was on par with press conferences held in the immediate wake of the scandal by then-captain Steve Smith and Warner. Loading Khawaja pulled out of interviews earlier this week after a bruising appearance on the ABC’s 7.30 on Tuesday night, when he refused to answer numerous questions, including what knowledge the now-captain Cummins had about sandpaper being used. World.content:

London’s Metropolitan Police are investigating new criminal allegations against disgraced comedian and convicted rapist Russell Brand as more women come forward with claims of sexual misconduct and rape. On Tuesday, Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Justice Joel Bennathan denounced the 51-year-old’s “casual and arrogant disregard” towards any woman who said no to him, and the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated back to 2004. Russell Brand arriving at court earlier this month. He was sentenced to more than a decade in prison for rape and sexual assault charges. Getty Images Since the sentencing, six women have come forward in an investigation by London’s The Times. One woman alleges Brand had sex with her without her consent and without a condom, then apologised after the alleged attack. Another woman said Brand continued to have sex with her despite her asking him to stop because it was hurting her.



“My body wasn’t ready for this, and it was painful,” she said, recalling the alleged incident to The Times. “An uneasy wave hits me, and I’m scared. And I say, ‘It’s painful,’ and he doesn’t stop. And then it gets worse, and it’s really painful. And I say, ‘Stop,’ and he doesn’t stop.” She alleges Brand later told her that “tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do.” Brand’s representatives did not respond to the new allegations. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame. Getty Images Meanwhile, London police said several people also contacted them following Brand’s trial and sentencing “to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation”, according to the BBC. Brand was already under investigation for two other alleged rapes during the trial, one involving a then-16-year-old girl.



The actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and behaviour on television and radio, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual. A jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six complainants. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison this week, while David Walliams (right) was identified as the star at the centre of another sexual misconduct investigation. Getty Images “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Justice Bennathan said. “You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

World.title: ‘We don’t need a deal’: Trump yanks JD Vance off Iran war talks
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war ‘We don’t need a deal’: Trump yanks JD Vance off Iran war talks Aamer Madhani November 13, 2026 — 9:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: US President Donald Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democrat-controlled cities and states. Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections in the US. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at Arlington National Cemetery in Washington this week. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post on Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said in the post. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”



Trump this week said that he believed the war “militarily is effectively over”, and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Vance’s message is loud and clear – Trump got it wrong Democrats have promised intense oversight of Trump’s business dealings and other targets when they take control of Congress in January after voters identified corruption as one of their top concerns. Trump’s post about Vance and the Iran war was, in part, responding to a flurry of reports about Democrats’ plans. But it also came after The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official. The vice president’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House press office responded to a query by highlighting that Trump made clear in his post that he sees no need to negotiate with Iran.



Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in US military interventions overseas, was lukewarm in his defence of the conflict after Trump launched it and became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting when he headed up negotiations over the summer. Following the election losses, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X in which he didn’t mince words about the political impact of the conflict. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance said. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” The vice president is considering whether to launch a 2028 run for the White House. Voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the war could weigh down those ambitions. The president has yet to endorse a successor for the 2028 race. In a CBS 60 Minutes interview that aired on Sunday, the president said he “may or may not get involved” in offering an endorsement.



Trump this week said that he believed that mediation efforts led by Qatar were making progress and that it was unlikely he would need to make good on earlier threats to restart the full-scale bombardment of Iran after he was past the midterm elections. Related Article US midterms These JD Vance challengers smell blood in the water after brutal midterms The president said on Thursday that he stood ready to restart strikes if necessary. “If something doesn’t work out, I would not hesitate,” he said. Oil shipments coming out of the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels after Iran effectively choked the critical waterway for months, stemming the flow of crude and energy resources from its Persian Gulf neighbours. But international tankers now are relying on US Navy escorts to get the oil out of the strait. The US military has recently carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defences.



And while crude and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf are climbing, there’s also been an uptick in attacks on ships trying to traverse the waterway. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week he pressed his Group of Seven counterparts during talks in Paris to “step up” and help protect ships from Iranian attacks but acknowledged making no headway on the issue. At the same time, a Saudi-led coalition is mired in fighting with Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. That fighting has made it precarious to transport oil and other goods through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. World.title: 30 years ago, the Spice Girls were global superstars. Now they swap parenting advice on a group chat
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCelebrity life 30 years ago, the Spice Girls were global superstars. Now they swap parenting advice on a group chat Gyan Yankovich November 13, 2026 — 10:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. If they weren’t one of the most famous girl groups in the world, the Spice Girls could almost be confused for any other female friendship group who met, and tightly bonded together for life, in their 20s. “Sporty Spice” Melanie C was 22 when the band’s debut single Wannabe was released, parachuting the group – which also included Victoria Beckham, Geri Halliwell, Emma Bunton and Mel B – into the global spotlight. Now 52, and promoting her Melanie C World Tour, visiting Australia this week, Melanie says the group’s friendships have only gotten better with age. Melanie C is performing in Sydney on Sunday. The Spice Girls – Posh, Baby, Scary, Ginger and Sporty – pictured in 1997. “The lovely thing now is – because we’re older – we’re just so much more relaxed and respectful of each other. I think, you know, when you’re maybe in your 20s and even into the 30s, there was a bit more infighting because we get frustrated with each other,” she says on the Good Weekend Talks podcast.



“But now it’s like a lot of peace and everyone’s mums, and I’m waiting for the first Spice Grandma to be honest – and it’s definitely going to be Victoria [Beckham], isn’t it?” 30 years ago, the Spice Girls changed the world of pop. Instagram In a conversation with Courtney Thompson on the Good Weekend Talks podcast, Melanie confirmed the group have not one, but “a few” group chats – different ones for different things. And while she remains closest to Bunton, Melanie – who has one daughter, 17-year-old Scarlett – says some of the best parenting advice she’s ever received came from Halliwell. “Geri said to me, ‘When Scarlett’s a teenager, she will need you even more than she needs you when she’s a toddler’. And I was thinking, ‘No way, your babies need you, right? Your babies need you’ [but] oh my gosh, she was so right.”



Melanie “Mel C” Chisholm with her Australian husband Chris Dingwall. Getty Images Listen to the full episode, where Melanie C reflects on the pressure she faced during the height of Spice mania, why she feels more confident in her own skin in her 50s than ever before, and the joy of getting behind the DJ decks. Now in her 50s and entering a new phase of her life and career, Melanie has been reflecting on the person she was when she rose to fame with the Spice Girls, and who she is today. She says the two versions of herself really aren’t that different.



Editor's pick Good Weekend Mel C met her future husband on a celebrity dating app. She reckons she hit the jackpot “We get really bombarded with who we should be, you know, what everybody’s expectation of us are, and I think it can just it can just wobble your core,” she says. “And the thing for me – which, you know, really changed everything – is literally realising I didn’t have to look outside myself to be who I am. It’s all very much rooted and there. “And I think that’s what’s so important about people who’ve known you since you were a kid, you know, family, the friends you grew up with at school ... Get them to remind you that you’re brilliant. “Who you were when you were 10 years old, is who you are when you’re 50 years old.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer, alleged double murderer’s cross-examination continues; grilled by Crown over texts to Jesse Baird
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial. The accused has returned to the witness box today for further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. There is no dispute that the men died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol on February 19, 2024, and that the accused disposed of the bodies on February 22, 2024.

Former NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, right, has denied murdering Luke Davies and Jesse Baird, whose bodies were found in Bungonia, near Goulburn. Instagram; Bungonia; Facebook

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon planned to kill Baird after developing an obsessive and jealous infatuation with him and that he killed Davies, Baird’s boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence. The 31-year-old has told the court he had his police pistol with him because he had contemplated taking his own life the previous night over work-related trauma.

This is the accused’s recent evidence:

He denied that he was referring to harming or killing Baird when he texted the former TV presenter on November 18, 2023: “You don’t need to worry about seeing me out etc because you won’t exist and no further conversation needs to take place.” Baird had broken up with him on November 16. The accused told the court that he was referring to acknowledging him only.

Lamarre-Condon said that it was partly true when he claimed he had cancer in a message he sent to Baird from his friend’s Instagram account later in November. A naturopathic doctor in Bondi Junction had told him at the end of October or early November 2023 that a lump on his shoulder appeared to be “a form of sporadic cancer”, he said.

He said the doctor recommended he get a biopsy. “I did not follow through with the biopsy,” he said. He said he did alternative therapies that he had sourced online.

He admitted to throwing Baird’s phone off a bridge to destroy potentially incriminating evidence after he died.

The accused also admitted to “gaslighting” Baird when he denied that he had posted an Instagram story on November 9, 2023, that falsely implied Baird had sent him flowers. He said he later admitted the truth. Lamarre-Condon told the court that he limited the audience for the story one person, namely, a man that Baird had been seeing at this time.

He rejected a suggestion by the prosecutor that his “unrequited love [for Baird] turned into an obsession”.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: I made my own mistake in 1981, and the shame is rarely about the act alone
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion I made my own mistake in 1981, and the shame is rarely about the act alone Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain November 13, 2026 — 10:09am

November 13, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve thought about Newlands more than I expected to. Not the footage, which we’ve all seen, but the feeling that came with it. It was heavy and familiar, the sense that Australian cricket had been walking towards something like this for a while, and that a lot of us had watched it happen and kept quiet. Trevor Chappell sends down his infamous underarm delivery to Brian McKechnie. Channel Nine I’m not writing as a bystander. I made my own mistake in 1981, and I’ve lived with it long enough to know the shame is rarely about the act alone. It’s about knowing you had the chance to be better but inexplicably slipped up. That’s what I saw in the faces of those young men at Newlands. Three young men, one terrible decision



Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for 12 months and Cameron Bancroft for nine. Smith and Warner were barred from leadership roles. They broke the rules and they knew it. Nobody should pretend otherwise, and none of them has. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images But I could never watch that press conference and see only wrongdoing. I saw a captain who couldn’t hold himself together and a young opener who looked like he wished the floor would swallow him. These weren’t hardened cheats. They were young men who’d picked up on what the surrounding environment rewarded, and they did something they deeply regret and will carry for the rest of their lives. Others from the 2018 squad can say for themselves what they knew. Some may remember it differently, and that’s their right.



The culture we built Simon Longstaff’s review found Cricket Australia and the national team had drifted into a culture where winning mattered more than almost anything. I read that and felt implicated. I was part of that world for most of my life, as a player, captain, coach and commentator. Test captain Pat Cummins addresses the media on Friday in an attempt to put the 2018 sandpaper scandal behind him. Getty Images We told ourselves that hard, fair cricket was Australian cricket. We admired the stare and the sledge and the refusal to give an inch, and we mistook ruthlessness for strength. Nobody sat down and decided to build a culture that would produce Newlands. It crept in. A decision defended because it worked. A line crossed and forgotten because the team won. A young player watching what the senior men let slide and what they cheered.



I wish more of us had said, much earlier, that this wasn’t who we wanted to be. Hard cricket and honest cricket aren’t opposites. The best Australian sides I saw were fiercely competitive and still respected the contest. Somewhere along the way we lost sight of that. What a single afternoon costs I know a bit about being defined by one decision. The underarm still comes up at dinners, in interviews, in letters from strangers, more than 45 years on. Loading I’m not after sympathy. I made the call and it was mine to own. But it’s shown me how long one moment can follow a person, and how little room people leave you to be more than the worst thing you’ve done.



Another perspective Exclusive

Ball tampering ‘You can’t say sandpaper’: Coach allegedly told Smith, Bancroft to lie That’s partly why the aftermath of Newlands sat so badly with me. There was a fair argument that the bans were too harsh, and a fair argument that they weren’t harsh enough for men wearing the baggy green. I could see both. What troubled me was the appetite. At times, it felt less like a demand for accountability and more like a hunger to watch someone fall. Smith rebuilt his career through hard work and humility. Bancroft has spoken honestly about what it did to him. Warner spent years asking for his leadership ban to be reviewed. None of them escaped the consequences, and none should have. But a game that talks so much about character ought to be able to hold two ideas at once: what happened was wrong, and people can earn their way back.



Dave Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft during the 2019 Ashes in England. Getty Images I have empathy and admiration for Usman Khawaja, for confronting this head on. That he’s done it after eight years doesn’t make it any less significant or any less true. And the suggestion that he’s doing it to sell a book? Anyone who says that either doesn’t know the publishing industry or doesn’t know Uzzy. Uzzy isn’t making it up. The lesson that’s easy to miss



Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, is published by Penguin Random House and available from November 10. It’s tempting to say Newlands was the fault of three men, and the game is cleaner today for having punished them. I don’t believe that. The harder lesson points back at the rest of us. Everyone at Newlands knew the rules. What failed was whatever sits underneath them, the instinct that tells you what you will and won’t do when nobody’s stopping you and winning is on the line. That instinct is learned. It’s taught by example, in dressing rooms and boardrooms, by what we reward and what we let slide. What I’d say to a young player now



I meet young people in cricket for whom one bad decision, or a run of bad luck, can mean losing everything. I tell them what I wish someone had told me: you’ll be tested on a day when you’re tired and under pressure, surrounded by people who want the same result you do. Knowing the rules won’t be enough that day. You’ll have to ask yourself what kind of person you want to be. I didn’t always ask. Those three young men didn’t ask at Newlands. And the culture, which I helped build, never taught them to. Cricket will always ask its players to compete with everything they’ve got. I’d only add that how you compete matters as much as whether you win. We learned that slowly, and at a cost. I hope we don’t have to learn it again. There has been enough said now about Newlands. Let us not disinter its bones.

Australian actor Chris Hemsworth’s Byron Bay home was broken into on Wednesday morning, and the thieves stole three vehicles from the property. Police were called to the Hollywood star’s Broken Head home, south of Byron Bay, about 7.30am following reports of a vehicle theft. According to a statement from NSW Police, officers attached to the Tweed-Byron Police District attended the scene, and were told four unknown people had entered the property and stolen three vehicles. No injuries were reported. Chris Hemsworth and wife Elsa Pataky in New York in 2024. AP “Police established a crime scene and commenced investigations into the circumstances surrounding the incident. Two of the vehicles were later recovered,” police said in a statement. According to a 7NEWS report, Hemsworth’s wife, Spanish actor and model Elsa Pataky, woke to the sound of dogs barking about 2am on Wednesday. She ignored the noise.



However, when she checked their property’s CCTV cameras later that morning, she reportedly saw four men wearing balaclavas and two of them holding knives. Hemsworth called police shortly after. The four men had reportedly scaled the front fence, gaining access to a garage where the three cars were parked with their keys inside, 7NEWS reported. The couple’s home in Broken Head, near Byron Bay. The stolen vehicles are reportedly a BYD, a Ram and a Ford Raptor ute, the report said. One of the vehicles was recovered at Coraki, which is about an hour’s drive away from Hemsworth’s home, and another at Tabulam, which is more than a two-hour’s drive away. “On Thursday, police recovered a third vehicle in Lennox Head. All of the cars have been seized for forensic examination, and inquiries are ongoing. Anyone with information is urged to contact the police.”



Related Article Wine & spirits ‘A defining moment’: Can Chris Hemsworth put Australian whisky on the world map? There have been no arrests and no charges. The Thor actor has lived in the Byron Bay area with his wife for more than a decade, having moved back to his homeland from Los Angeles in 2014. Their luxury property, often described as “Fortress Hemsworth”, looks out over Seven Mile Beach and is reportedly worth around $50 million. Speaking on the SmartLess podcast in February, Hemsworth explained why he chose to relocate his family – which includes his three children – back to Australia. “It was right around the time my boys were born, and we kind of were set up in LA and not enjoying it,” he said. “Nothing was shooting there, we were filming kind of everywhere else.”



He also spoke of disliking the constant media attention and paparazzi associated with living in Los Angeles as a celebrity. Moving back to Australia had been the “greatest decision”, he said. Chris Hemsworth most recently starred as a jewel thief alongside Mark Ruffalo in Crime 101. AP “You know when you come back from work you want to go on a holiday? Coming home for me feels like a holiday … We have a big farm and horses and motorbikes and surf.” Hemsworth’s most recent film was Crime 101, Amazon MGM’s crime thriller in which the 43-year-old played a jewel thief. He will reprise his role as Thor in Avengers: Doomsday in December. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: ‘Khawaja is 100 per cent wrong’: Pat Cummins responds to sandpaper revelations
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Khawaja is 100 per cent wrong’: Pat Cummins responds to sandpaper revelations Jack Gramenz, Frances Howe and Tom Decent November 13, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australia’s Test cricket captain Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja is “100 per cent wrong” to say bowlers knew sandpaper was being used to rough up the ball during matches on the tour of South Africa in 2018. Former Test batsman Khawaja this week alleged “all of us” knew sandpaper was being used to rough up the ball during the 2018 tour, despite several players, notably the bowlers, having denied this in one of the biggest scandals in Australian cricketing history. Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins during an appearance on Friday. Sam Mooy Cummins said on Friday he’s taken his time “trying to understand exactly what” Khawaja has alleged, saying some of his claims are “probably true” “But I think there’s a few big leaps here, where he’s being vague … the details really matter,” he said.



“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100 per cent wrong. “I did not know that was happening.” Media prepare ahead of Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins appearance at Cricket Central in Sydney. Sam Mooy “[Khawaja] says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.” Cummins said he supported Khawaja’s “right to tell a story” and described Khawaja as a friend.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Khawaja cancels book interviews after refusing to answer key question about Cummins “But friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations.” When Cameron Bancroft was captured on camera putting a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 Test in Cape Town, Cummins was 24, playing his 13th Test “in a team that at that stage I think had a win at all cost mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there was too many silos within the team,” Cummins said. “Traits that I hope that everyone’s seen, and I tried very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain.” Following Khawaja’s claims, a key figure involved in a player review after the scandal subsequently called on Cricket Australia to reopen an investigation into the use of sandpaper in 2018.



David Warner, vice-captain at the time and one of three players suspended over the incident, described Khawaja’s version of events as 100 per cent accurate. Interest in the scandal’s resurgence this week has only grown as the days went on. The media turnout for Cummins on Friday was on par with press conferences held in the immediate wake of the scandal by then-captain Steve Smith and Warner. Loading Khawaja pulled out of interviews earlier this week after a bruising appearance on the ABC’s 7.30 on Tuesday night, when he refused to answer numerous questions, including what knowledge the now-captain Cummins had about sandpaper being used. Russell Brand arriving at court earlier this month. He was sentenced to more than a decade in prison for rape and sexual assault charges. Close Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democrat-controlled cities and states. Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections in the US. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at Arlington National Cemetery in Washington this week. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post on Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said in the post. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”



Trump this week said that he believed the war “militarily is effectively over”, and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Vance’s message is loud and clear – Trump got it wrong Democrats have promised intense oversight of Trump’s business dealings and other targets when they take control of Congress in January after voters identified corruption as one of their top concerns. Trump’s post about Vance and the Iran war was, in part, responding to a flurry of reports about Democrats’ plans. But it also came after The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official. The vice president’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House press office responded to a query by highlighting that Trump made clear in his post that he sees no need to negotiate with Iran.



Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in US military interventions overseas, was lukewarm in his defence of the conflict after Trump launched it and became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting when he headed up negotiations over the summer. Following the election losses, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X in which he didn’t mince words about the political impact of the conflict. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance said. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” The vice president is considering whether to launch a 2028 run for the White House. Voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the war could weigh down those ambitions. The president has yet to endorse a successor for the 2028 race. In a CBS 60 Minutes interview that aired on Sunday, the president said he “may or may not get involved” in offering an endorsement.



Trump this week said that he believed that mediation efforts led by Qatar were making progress and that it was unlikely he would need to make good on earlier threats to restart the full-scale bombardment of Iran after he was past the midterm elections. Related Article US midterms These JD Vance challengers smell blood in the water after brutal midterms The president said on Thursday that he stood ready to restart strikes if necessary. “If something doesn’t work out, I would not hesitate,” he said. Oil shipments coming out of the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels after Iran effectively choked the critical waterway for months, stemming the flow of crude and energy resources from its Persian Gulf neighbours. But international tankers now are relying on US Navy escorts to get the oil out of the strait. The US military has recently carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defences.



And while crude and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf are climbing, there’s also been an uptick in attacks on ships trying to traverse the waterway. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week he pressed his Group of Seven counterparts during talks in Paris to “step up” and help protect ships from Iranian attacks but acknowledged making no headway on the issue. At the same time, a Saudi-led coalition is mired in fighting with Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. That fighting has made it precarious to transport oil and other goods through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. World.title: KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals hit record levels, but some could be avoided
World.content:
A researcher says if governments want to look at making Kiwisaver changes, they should also look at the high increase of hardship withdrawals.

A Victoria University report led by senior lecturer of law Victoria Stace, and commissioned by FinCap shows hardship withdrawals rose sharply in the 12 months to June 2026.

More than 52,000 KiwiSaver members withdrew, which is up from just over 20,000 in 2023.

Total hardship withdrawals have increased from $65 million in 2016 to $443.6m in 2025 and Inland Revenue said the withdrawals now outpace withdrawals for first home deposits.

Stace told Nine to Noon concern over the increase in hardship withdrawals had been expressed by various groups including Retirement Commission, Consumer New Zealand and Financial Markets Authority.

Audio player for " KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals not always necessary: report " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2574701%2Fkiwisaver-hardship-withdrawals-hit-record-levels-but-some-could-be-avoided

KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals not always necessary: report Nine To Noon Download MP3 20m

This helped launch the research report which interviewed stakeholders, financial mentors and Kiwisaver providers and looked into superanuation arrangements around the world.

Stace said the research found that those who make KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals often would not have done so had they been made aware of other support options.

Kiwisaver contributions have been a part of the recent elections with both major parties proposing policies.

National proposed increasing contributions up to 12 percent total and making it compulsory for both the employer and employee. Labour's policy would not make it compulsory for the employee.

Stace said if any party was making changes it was an opportunity to look at other issues regarding hardship withdrawals.

"I think the main issue is if the government's serious about helping people get through times of hardship without accessing their KiwiSaver, then they seriously need to consider how that's going to be funded and how financial mentors are going to be incorporated into the process in a way that is sustainable and recognise the value that they can provide in this space."

Lilley said their research showed that financial mentors were concerned if these policies go into place and more money is going into Kiwisaver it would lead to more people looking to take Kiwisaver out.

He said there were around 750 financial mentors with at least 318 full-time equivalents worth of work.

Of those 318 around 181.5 were funded by the Ministry of Social Development. Lilley said this showed a "chronic underfunding " of the sector.

What are the options?

"There are a number of options, whether it's an intermediate step or, I mean, for example, you could have that it was a requirement that you'd spoken to a financial mentor as part of your application process," Stace said.

She said another option was to have all financial hardship withdrawal applications processed by a central clearinghouse or hub, which has financial mentoring expertise built into it.

This was a model already used by six of Kiwisaver providers, Stace said.

She explained applications were made to the Kiwisaver provider who then put a formal application to the supervisor. There were three supervisors, the main one being public trust, who make the final decision.

FinCap's senior policy advisor Jake Lilley says there needs a to be a system where budget advisors can be involved and check all options before a hardship withdrawal.

"You might have entitlement at, say, working income or another government agency or local charity you weren't aware of, or it had been hard to navigate in the first place, that actually means you can get on top of things.

"Sometimes people have had their consumer rights breached and actually there's an underlying issue or they have options."

The average hardship withdrawal amount had been $10,000

Stace said the report also found that the idea of "sidecar savings" should be explored which means setting aside money in a Kiwisaver account ring-fenced for an emergency.
