World.title: Christopher Luxon to attend APEC summit in China in caretaker capacity
World.content:
The prime minister will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China next week, with the government making arrangements to attend in a caretaker capacity.

The APEC leaders' meeting will take place in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November, with the likes of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin all expected to be there.

Christopher Luxon will be accompanied by Trade Minister Todd McClay.

Meanwhile, Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters will attend the East Asia Summit in the Philippines, on November 16 and 17.

While the country waits for the special votes to come in, the government is operating under the caretaker convention, meaning the opposition was consulted on the visits.

During the election campaign, Luxon said an assessment would be made on New Zealand's representation after the election, and he had told China's premier Li Qiang he was "not 100 percent sure" he would be there himself.

It is not unusual for governments to make caretaker arrangements at major international summits during election years.

In 2023, New Zealand was represented at APEC by Labour's outgoing trade minister Damien O'Connor in a caretaker capacity, while Luxon focused on forming a government.

The same year, Carmel Sepuloni attended the Pacific Islands Forum leaders' meeting in Fiji, with National's Gerry Brownlee attending plenary sessions as the government-elect representative.

Ministers did not attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, with New Zealand represented by Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials instead.

World.title: New Plymouth-built storage tanks headed for Australian fertiliser plant
World.content:
Audio player for " Taranaki engineering sector gets a boost from tank exports " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2567835%2Fnew-plymouth-built-storage-tanks-headed-for-australian-fertiliser-plant

Taranaki engineering sector gets a boost from tank exports Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The export of three massive ammonia storage tanks from New Plymouth is being heralded as evidence the Taranaki engineering sector still has a future.

Built by Dialog Fitzroy for Hiringa Energy, the 35-metre long, 3.5-metre diameter, 100-tonne pressure vessels have been transported across town at night this week to Port Taranaki, before shipping to Australia.

As a huge ammonia bullet approaches on State High 3 amid a blaze of flashing lights and pouring rain, its scale becomes immediately apparent.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408289076112

Standing more than 5m high, it's carried on a 12 axle trailer - six axles each end with an 8m spacer - and it seems to go on forever.

Jarvis Miller of PTS Logistics is behind the wheel.

PTS Logistics driver Jarvis Miller said navigating such a long load was challenging. RNZ / Robin Martin

"The length of it is one of the key issues. It's 36m long, so that's just over a standard truck-and-a-half's length, without being able to turn in the centre.

"The total length of the unit is about 56m, because the average truck is about 21m."

Supplied

He is about to take the load over a bypass ramp built especially for similar transports headed out to the 'Think Big' project at Motunui in the mid-1980s.

"It's a bit of a greasy night, and it's all wet and slippery, so we're hooking up another truck just to give us a little more power over the climb here.

"All up, we're about 215 tonne, with just the main truck. One truck won't quite do it, so we've got another one on standby."

The pressure vessels are on their way to Hiringa Energy's $120 million Good Earth Green Hydrogen and Ammonia project in Moree, New South Wales.

Chief executive Andrew Clennett says they will be used in Australasia's first green fertiliser production plant.

Hiringa CE Andrew Clennett says the partnership with Dialog Fitzroy is an example of what Taranaki firms can achieve when they work together. RNZ / Robin Martin

"We have a large solar farm, we have some batteries, and obviously, the sun goes up and down, and it stores that energy and we feed it into an electrolyzer that makes hydrogen.

"Then we take that hydrogen and turn that, combined with nitrogen from the air, into ammonia, which is what goes into these bullets."

He says the partnership with Dialog Fitzroy is a perfect example of what Taranaki companies can do on an international stage.

"They are out there helping us lay out all the equipment coming in, helping us tie it in... all the pipework to bring it together.

"Utilising all the expertise that we've developed over years of activity here in Taranaki, bringing in modules from international, and getting really good at placing and them hooking them up, and making sure that's done safely and efficiently, and it works." .

Dialog Fitzroy general manager Doug Timanus says such projects are vital for retaining skilled workers in the province.

Dialog Fitzroy project manager Shareece Kahukaka-Taylor and general manager Doug Timanus. RNZ / Robin Martin

"It's important for Taranaki and New Zealand, as well as Dialog Fitzroy, because it's very competitive trying to do something like this in New Zealand, rather in Asia, and like Andrew said, the skillset is going out of tradespeople and apprentices, so it is really important and we've been really lucky to be involved."

Meanwhile, Miller reflects on a cool cruise across town.

"There were a couple of corners where we turned at a 90-degree angle, but it's not only the angle, it's the change in elevation of the road, and because it is such a long load, we have to lift and lower the suspension, so it doesn't bottom out.

"It's a bit of fun, especially on a night like tonight, but I enjoy it. This is what I live for."

World.title: Voters in areas with large Pacific populations clear on who should lead country
World.content:
Justin Latif - RNZ Pacific News Editor

While the general election result might be too close to call, Labour has again drawn strong support from communities with a large Pacific voter base.

National and Labour finished in a near dead heat for the party vote - with Labour on 29.4 percent percent and National on 29.2 percent, but with almost 400,000 special votes still to be tallied, who can form a coalition is not yet certain.

Based on preliminary results it's fairly clear there will be eight Pacific members of Parliament (MPs), increasing representation in the previous term from seven.

And for those Pacific Labour MPs who won their electorates, support for many of them has also significantly increased since 2023 - assuming special votes don't swing back to the right.

Labour's Barbara Edmonds, who is of Samoan descent, won Kenepuru with 17,294 votes, almost ten-thousand more than the next best placed candidate (which she won by 7324 votes in 2023 when the electorate was called Mana) and fellow Samoan Lemauga Lydia Sosene regained Māngere with 14,815 votes and an increased 11,970 margin (having previous won by 11,712).

Three-term Tongan MP Jenny Salesa is also back, winning Ōtāhuhu for Labour with 13,826 votes with a margin of over ten-thousand (having previously won by 7,970) and Labour's Samoan-Tongan deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni won Glendene with 14,478 votes with a 6,940 margin (having won by 4,396 when her electorate was previously called Kelston).

Labour's Tangi Utikere, who is Cook Islands descent, also retained his seat of Palmerston North with a similar margin as 2023, while fellow Cook Islander and former National Party minister Alfred Ngaro re-enters Parliament after a six year absence, but this time under the NZ First banner thanks to his fifth place ranking on its list.

The Greens won 13.3% of the party vote according to preliminary results, meaning Teanau Tuiono, who is of Cook Islands descent, returns to Parliament thanks to his third place ranking, while first-time MP Tania Waikato, who's of Māori, Samoan and Hawaiian heritage, also enters due to her list placing of 13.

None of National's three Pacific list candiates of Rosemary Bourke, Angee Nicholas and Agnes Loheni will make it into Parliament, given their party's lower party vote percentage and the unusual situation where the party won 42 electorates - creating an overhang

Fania Kapao, Labour Party volunteer who is Cook Islands and Samoan descent at one of Labour's post-election events on November 7, 2026. RNZ Pacific/ Justin Latif

Pacific Labour voters react

While election night didn't fall strongly in Labour's favour, it was clear for Pacific voters at Labour's post-election event in Tamaki why their support swung left.

For Rua Rio and Koro Tuarae, Cook Islanders from Glen Innes, Labour was who they felt would do the most to address the cost of living.

"There's a lot of things we've seen that this government has been doing that makes it hard," Tuarae said.

"Things like the length of stay with hospital, there's [a shortage of] nurses, doctors and so when you go to hospital you can sit there for so many hours before they see you."

For Rio, the lack of jobs and the price of petrol were two factors in his support for a left-wing government.

"It's so hard to get a job now because three years ago I had a factory job, but it was closed but I know if Labour comes on board, people always work aye."

While failure to turn around cost of living pressures during this term has hurt the National Party electorally, its finance spokseperson told the public that the signs of a turnaround in the economy are starting to appear.

Nicola Willis, who has not made it back into parliament, said that the National-led coalition has been laying the foundations for a economic rebound during trying times, but that improvement can take time.

Labour's Tamaki candidate Max Harris, left, with a campaign volunteer at his post-election event on November 7, 2026. RNZ Pacific/ Justin Latif

Fania Kapao, who is of Cook Islands and Samoan descent, volunteered for Labour in Glendene. She felt excited to see more young people involved in this campaign than in previous years even though overall voter turn out was down almost 4 percent from last election.

"I hope that Pacific people feel a lot more represented and seen [by this result]," Kapao said.

"And I'm feeling very hopeful with the new and fresh blood that's coming through."

For Gloria Tu'itupou, a 24-year-old Tongan-New Zealander youth leader, she was inspired by how Labour's Tamaki candidate Max Harris engaged the Pacific community in her neighbourhood.

"I loved what Max Harris has been doing, centring Pacific communities in Glen Innes and Point England," she said.

"I like that he's been out and about in the community and talking to heaps of people in the community about what problems we have been facing, especially because our problems might get overshadowed by the wealthier areas."

She was also concerned how the turnout was impacted by the decision to scrap same-day voter enrollment.

"I feel like the way that they've set it up not being able to enrol and vote on the same day really impacts a lot of our communities.

"Our Pacific communities are more disenfranchised by this government and that's what motivated me to get out and be a bit more vocal.

World.title: British Airways plane suffers tail strike as it attempts landing at London's Heathrow Airport
World.content:
A dramatic tail strike incident has been caught on camera at London's Heathrow Airport.

The aircraft involved was an Airbus A321neo, operated by British Airways.

The plane, which can carry about 200 passengers, had flown from Amsterdam and was touching down on the runway at Europe's busiest airport when its rear appeared to strike the ground twice.

Embedded content removed for printing https://x.com/BigJetTVLIVE/status/2120865653431402927

The cockpit crew then aborted the landing and climbed away from the airport.

A second landing attempt was successful, with no incident.

The tail strike incident was captured on a YouTube livestream operated by FlightRadar24 and Big Jet TV.

At this stage, the aircraft involved is not scheduled to fly again for another two days.

A British Airways spokesperson said: "The aircraft landed safely and we're assisting the AAIB with its investigation and are legally unable to comment further at this stage."

World.title: Fire and Emergency considers how to cover for striking fire crews
World.content:
Audio player for " Megan Stiffler discusses firefighter strike plans " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/emergencies_national/2567052%2Ffire-and-emergency-considers-how-to-cover-for-striking-fire-crews

Megan Stiffler discusses firefighter strike plans Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Fire and Emergency is looking at how the Defence Force could help but has made no formal request two weeks' out from an unprecedented 10-hour Friday afternoon strike by most paid firefighters.

FENZ is instead relying primarily on volunteer firefighters if the first strike goes ahead on 27 November, national commander Megan Stiffler told Morning Report on Friday.

The other main response would be putting out safety messages to the community, she said.

FENZ has settled on this approach following a month of talks "across government" on how to keep the public as safe as possible.

An early options plan to put Defence Force firefighters on FENZ trucks at up to 20 key fire stations had been dropped.

"We would never put another workforce in our fire stations," Stiffler said.

"The Defence Force has very limited capability to assist us. We are talking to them about what they could do with regards to engineering if we have a building collapse of some sort.

"They can assist us if we have a capability of an issue that our volunteers cannot deliver."

A contingency plan received by the volunteer firefighters' United Fire Brigades Association from FENZ on Wednesday does not mention Defence, only "partner agency support".

Audio player for " Defence Force involved in plans for firefighter strikes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/emergencies_national/2567052%2Ffire-and-emergency-considers-how-to-cover-for-striking-fire-crews

Defence Force involved in plans for firefighter strikes Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The association and FENZ both said volunteers might be called in to fight fires in areas paid crews would normally cover, but would not be asked to do anything other than what they currently do.

That means during a 10-hour strike there would be no use of the larger ladder-trucks (often used on high-rises or at industrial fires), or chemical spill cleanup and no complex extrication of people from road crashes ('jaws of life'), said statements.

"There are significant gaps in the emergency response ... that simply cannot be filled," FENZ told RNZ.

It was "exploring all potential options" and working with NZDF, police, ambulance and the National Emergency Management Agency NEMA on that.

The NZDF said there had been no agreements or formal requests for support made yet, "however the NZDF is conducting contingency planning" with FENZ.

The Defence Minister had received no request from FENZ for help, said the minister's office.

Both FENZ and the Professional Firefighters' Union blame each other for the impacts, with the former saying the strikes could have fatal consequences.

David Phillips, a senior firefighter in central Auckland and union member told Morning Report on Friday it would not be safe for Defence firefighters to be used in places or operations they were not trained for.

Stiffler agreed saying "This is a big gap in our capability and you can't replicate that quickly".

While NZDF told RNZ, "NZDF personnel would have to conduct a period of familiarisation training if they were to provide support in an unfamiliar area or use unfamiliar equipment."

It would support FENZ in a way that lets it maintain fire cover at its own camps and bases, it said.

But Phillips also said volunteer crews lacked specialist fire trucks and sometimes specialist training. "One of the core tenants of being a career firefighter and a volunteer firefighter is that we do the work that we're trained to do.

"And they're not in the locations where the most calls happen - those 20 percent of the firefighters who are paid respond to 80 percent of the calls."

FENZ said no crew would attend an incident without a senior officer in support.

"We have written to employers indicating a possible increased activity for our volunteers/their employees," it said.

Phillips said FENZ should be focused on putting a fair offer on the table to stop the strike.

Stiffler said other leaders were working on that.

"Head of people and our CE and the board chair is focusing on a resolution to settling this agreement.

"There's no guarantee we can get settlement by the 27th, so as the lead of operations for New Zealand my focus is on contingency planning."

World.title: ‘I just couldn’t get it out of my brain’: Kaikōura quake remembered 10 years on
World.content:
Audio player for " Kaikoura earthquake survivors reflect ten years on " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions_canterbury/2566467%2Fi-just-couldn-t-get-it-out-of-my-brain-kaikoura-quake-remembered-10-years-on

Kaikoura earthquake survivors reflect ten years on Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Gary Morton and his partner Jo-Anne MacKinnon spent the night watching an Adam Sandler movie before heading to bed at home in Mt Lyford on the night the Kaikōura earthquake struck.

Morton got up to let their dog out when the violent 7.8 magnitude quake hit shortly after midnight on 14 November 2016.

"She was following me and then, bang, my house went up two-and-a-half metres in the air," he said.

Morton was thrown out of the door and felt MacKinnon collide with his back.

"I still had the damn Sky remote in my hand and I was bouncing up and down, it went for about two minutes, 20 seconds or something, which is a long time."

When the shaking stopped, Morton went inside and yelled out for MacKinnon. The power had gone out and he could not see her.

"I started the car up and backed that out and put the lights into the doorway and there she was lying on the ground," he said.

"I tried to bring her back to life as best I could."

Gary Morton and Jo-Anne MacKinnon. Supplied / Gary Morton

MacKinnon died in his arms. It was 14 hours before anyone reached the couple.

"It was just awful. I kept having this nightmare all the time, just this non-stop nightmare. I could have saved her, if this had happened, if that had happened, I kept reliving it. I just couldn't get it out of my brain," he said.

Morton rebuilt the log cabin in Mt Lyford but was diagnosed with cancer not long after the earthquake and decided to move to Christchurch.

"We were just made for each other. I needed somebody strong, and God, she was strong," he said.

"I just loved her so much."

Albert Louis Edgar, 74, also died in the quake when he was struck by falling debris and crushed to death in his Elms Homestead, while dozens of other people were injured.

Jo-Anne MacKinnon died in the Kaikōura earthquake. Supplied / Gary Morton

Widespread damage to road and rail

Near the coast, KiwiRail locomotive engineer Wayne Sullivan was driving a freight train south towards Kaikōura when it started to bang around and move from side to side.

"As I approached the tunnel I could see sort of silt and dust falling from the ceiling and it made me realise it was an earthquake. I was like, 'okay, throw the brake on and stop because this is pretty big'. I didn't want to keep going not knowing what the condition of the track was in ahead of me," he said.

Sullivan thought the Alpine Fault was rupturing.

The engine came to a stop on the other side of the tunnel where Sullivan sat in the cab while hundreds of aftershocks hit.

At one point, he tried to clear some rocks off the road.

"I thought I'd be doing drivers a service by clearing the road a little bit so that no one crashed into them, not knowing that the whole State Highway had basically collapsed in different parts," he said.

Sullivan thought the biggest threat was a tsunami, so kept an eye on the sea in case it receded. After receiving an official tsunami warning, train control told him to get to higher ground.

He was picked up by a helicopter around 7am and, flying south, saw a massive pile of debris on the track near Ohau Point, which made him realise the scale of the damage and how lucky he had been to stop where he did.

Kaikoura earthquake, tracks ripped from their beds in the quake. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

The main north line was so badly damaged that KiwiRail staff said they were not sure if repairs would be possible. The track was buried by slips and landslides in more than 100 places.

KiwiRail and the New Zealand Transport Agency then joined forces to create North Canterbury Transport Infrastructure Recovery, which brought in contractors and engineering consultants to help restore road and rail links.

At the height of the operation, around 1000 people were working on the rebuild from the Kaikōura area.

KiwiRail general manager of project delivery Daniel Headifen said there were more than 1000 points of damage along the main north line after the quake.

"That was the real question, is the damage too big to even consider reopening the line? The next question after that was, if you couldn't reopen that line, what becomes of the South Island railway?" he said.

Some rail tunnels were completely buried by slips, in other places the track had been picked up and thrown 50 to 100 metres into the sea.

Ten months later the line was re-established in one of the biggest rail restoration projects ever completed. Restricted freight resumed in September 2017 and the first post-earthquake passenger train ran in December 2018.

The road reopening took a little longer, with State Highway 1 north of Kaikōura opening one year, one month and one day after the quake.

Major slips on State highway 1, north of Kaikoura, in 2016. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

'Cow island' makes international headlines

Derrick Millton was in St Arnaud that night and as more details came in about the quake over the radio, he knew he had to get home to his farm near the Clarence River mouth.

"We were the first car into the Kaikōura coast coming south from Ward and we had to dodge bridges that had poked out of the tar seal. At one place at Tirohanga straight there was a metre-wide gap in the road and we had to pick up a whole lot of pieces of tar seal and fill the gap up so we could hop over it, so we made the road as we went south," he said.

Millton said the damage to Waipapa Farm, which is now owned by his son, was significant.

"From north of Kekerengu we could see how much damage there was. The whole hillside had fallen down and because it's limestone, it was showing up as a white face. We knew that there were 600 sheep on that block and clearly they must have known what was going on before the earthquake because they had sort of removed themselves off the steep part and we lost surprisingly few," he said.

Around 12 kilometres of fencing on the farm needed to be straightened out, and farmers came from around the district to help.

Cracks along the Kekerengu Fault. Supplied / GNS Science

Millton's cows and a calf made headlines around the world with an aerial photo of the animals stranded on an island of grass after their paddock was ripped apart.

He said they were in a state of total shock.

"The cows were scared, they were really suffering from the earthquake and they just stood behind the guys who were trying to rescue them and didn't do anything other than stop and wait for the track to be cleared," he said.

Early on, then-Kaikoura mayor Winston Gray said the extent of the damage was not clear.

"At that time of the day, we were thinking we'd be closed up for a couple of weeks, we weren't aware of what was required and that the road north would be closed for so long," he said.

"We had so many people here in town to get out, that was one of the major problems."

Tourists in the quake-stricken town were evacuated by helicopter and others on HMNZS Canterbury to Lyttleton.

Gray said it was a struggle for many people in Kaikōura, at the beginning of the busy summer season, with the road shut and fewer tourists around.

"To be stuck like that, it was a real challenge, but the government at the time, they were pretty good, they acted really quick to help people," he said.

The help included a $17.5 million business support package for people in Kaikōura, Hurunui and Wellington, paired with $5m in primary sector support and tourism advertising/wage subsidies.

Additional funding was granted to restore the harbour at South Bay, pay off the Kaikōura Health Centre loan, support waste and debris management and to commission marine recovery research.

'Kind of unprecedented'

Earth Sciences NZ earthquake geologist Kate Clark. RNZ / Andrew McRae

Earth Sciences NZ earthquake geologist Kate Clark said the earthquake struck within the Marlborough fault system, which lies between the Alpine Fault and Hikurangi Subduction Zone.

It started near the North Canterbury town of Waiau and ruptured around 20 different faults, all the way to Cape Campbell on the coast.

"A lot of earthquakes just rupture one fault, this ruptured over 20, so it was kind of unprecedented in how many faults it actually managed to jump across and rupture. Those faults were both onshore and offshore and a few faults ruptured on the seafloor as well," she said.

Clark said scientists were still learning from the remarkably complex quake to understand the plate boundary movement across the faults, to determine which took most of the action from the Alpine Fault.

She said a lot of work had been done to understand how the faults were linked to each other and at what depths.

"Why did this earthquake grow to be so large, rupture so many faults, why didn't it just stop as a small magnitude 6.5 down in Canterbury, what enabled it to propagate and grow larger and larger as it linked up lots of faults as it travelled to the north?" she said.

Clark hoped the research would enable better forecasting of future earthquakes in similar settings.

World.title: Live: Cummins hits out at Khawaja claims as 'complete and utter nonsense'
World.content:
(AAP)

Pat Cummins said yesterday he has "taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly".

Nothing wrong with wrapping your head around what's been said to avoid going off media reports, but in the meantime a lot of his past and present teammates have been doing media opps and been forced to answer questions about it.

The party line from current players has pretty much been: "Usman's told his story, which he's entitled to do, but I'm not keen to relitigate the events of 2018."

If that's all Cummins offers this morning, this could be a very frustrating morning for him and reporters.

When the prospect of Khawaja's book came out, Cummins revealed they had spoken ahead of time and the skipper said:

"It's obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times. It was dealt with then. All I can say is as a group we've moved on. [I'm] very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we've been as a group and evolved. He didn't go into too much detail … As always, it was, 'No worries. You can tell your story. That's fine.'"

The issue is, while Khawaja's book tells the story from his perspective, it's not only his story because it does implicate others. Whether that's saying an unnamed assistant coach called for more work on the ball, or implying an unnamed fast bowler knew more than has been let on, or shedding more light on the conduct of David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, these are Khawaja's stories but they're ABOUT others.

Cummins was there and now, eight years later, he's the captain of this Test team. It would be good if we could have a few more answers than the usual, but I'm not overly optimistic to be honest.

World.title: Sixers win WBBL clash despite Ellyse Perry's strange run-out
World.content:
New Zealand captain Melie Kerr has starred with the bat and ball to keep the Sydney Sixers unbeaten in the WBBL with a victory over the Melbourne Renegades.

In the second match of a double-header at Melbourne's Junction Oval, Kerr set up the Sixers' 11-run win by top-scoring with 53 off 34 balls and finishing with tidy figures of 1-29.

It lifted the Sixers to 5-0 at the season's halfway mark and into second spot alongside the also unbeaten Perth Scorchers.

Kerr was the only batter to pass 50 in the game, sharing a crucial 56-run partnership with opener Ellyse Perry before the Australian star was undone in unusual circumstances.

In the 18th over, Kerr chipped a ball into the deep on the leg side and pushed for two, with Perry as Georgia Wareham swooped on the ball in the deep and fired it into the bowler's end.

Sophie Molineux fielded cleanly and whipped the bails off as Perry dove to make her ground, and there was only half an appeal from the Renegades to umpire Louise Broadfoot, who shook her head.

Former Australia captain Lisa Sthalekar in commentary credited Broadfoot and fellow caller Aaron Finch prophetically said: "There must be something in the back of the umpire's mind that goes 'what if I just haven't quite got it right though?'."

As the slow-motion replay on the big screen at Junction Oval showed Perry's dive bouncing over the line, rather than being grounded, the crowd and everyone on the field raised their eyebrows, with Broadfoot consulting fellow umpire Malcolm Wood before sending it to the third umpire.

Perry had already started making her way off the field before the decision was made, with her team adding 16 in the final two overs to set up the chase.

As the pitch slowed, the Renegades got off to a horror start chasing 141 to win after collapsing to 3-22 by the fifth over.

Molineux inched her way to 18 off 21 and was livid when caught trying to cut away Caoimhe Bray (1-17), but Tess Flintoff (44 off 33) breathed life back into the Renegades.

Needing 17 off the last over to win, spinner Ashleigh Gardner (3-13 off three overs) shut the door as the Renegades were bowled out for 129.

In the earlier game, a captain's knock from Georgia Redmayne propelled Brisbane past the Melbourne Stars and into the top four.

Set 166 for victory, skipper Redmayne (74 not out off 50 deliveries) and Irish young gun Orla Prendergast (52 not out off 36) put the Stars to the sword.

It was the Stars' fourth straight loss, while the Heat are sitting pretty in third with three victories on the bounce after going 706 days without a triumph.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: AFLW has come a long way but this player 'doesn’t want to settle'
World.content:
When Jenna Richardson scrolls through TikTok, she's now starting to come across AFLW content — and lots of it.

To the inaugural Hawthorn defender, it's a sign of the game's evolution and how it's connecting to fans.

"There are videos of people analysing the games … It's nice because they analyse the men's game, so then to see them do it for the W, [it's good]," Richardson tells ABC Sport.

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

After securing Hawthorn's first finals win last week (against Gold Coast), the side are now gearing up for a semi-final against Carlton on Saturday at Princes Park, a ground that drew 5,000 fans for the weekend's prior qualifying finals.

This season, the overall AFLW home-and-away attendance record was broken in round 10, helped by the introduction of double-headers, with the two crowds at Docklands drawing 20,455 and 14,573, respectively.

Excluding the matches with men's games, standalone games were at an average of 2,500 per game, similar to the 2025 figures.

"I'm pretty level-headed in being able to see the games come a long way," Richardson said.

"So whilst I am so grateful for everything we get, and I feel quite spoiled at times, I also know there's a lot of room for growth — and not to settle."

The biggest change Richardson wants to see is the number of regular season rounds increase from 12 — which she really feels during finals.

Hawthorn are the only team to have beaten North Melbourne in three years. (Getty: Emily Barker)

"At least playing every team once to make a more realistic ladder at the end of the season," she said.

Every team's fixture is dependent on where they finished the year before, meaning sides that finished lower theoretically play more fellow-lower sides, and vice versa with the top sides.

It can result in some teams making finals that get caught out straight away, and some that could make a finals run with more rounds, missing out.

"Playing the top teams, we always get the most out of… the more you play the best teams, the better you becomel. We did," Richardson said, noting Hawthorn were the only team to beat North Melbourne in three years.

"We played Adelaide (not in finals) and got beat. I thought they were really good to play against.

"They have shown in the past, for however many years, that they're up for finals contention. I feel like if there were more games, I wouldn't be surprised if they were in there too."

Hawthorn are playing in its first semi-finals in AFLW history. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Richardson said, she'd then like to see increased salaries for support staff and assistant coaches in women's programs.

Richardson notes how stretched programs can be, which adds pressure on coaches, assistant coaches and support staff.

"They [line coaches] sacrifice a lot from their other jobs, like they're usually losing money to come and help our program," she said.

"They have to do so much for us... (and) those two days a week where they're at our club, they're taking a massive pay cut from their other job."

Jenna Richardson joined Hawthorn as an expansion signing in 2022. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

With the W awards coming up, Richardson is also not opposed to the introduction of a defender award, given the best and fairest generally goes to a midfielder and there is a medal for leading goalkicker.

"Why not?" Richardson asked.

"That'd actually be cool because we're never in those, you know, fun photos or celebrating goals that are down there — so that'd be fun."

World.title: Are we really going to shoot the messenger over Sandpapergate?
World.content:
Consider a famous scene from the heat of a Test cricket battle. The South African team manager calls the opposition chairman of selectors into a room and says: "You'd better have a look at this." The pair sit down to view some sinister television footage.

The chairman of selectors is aghast at the replays: something comes out of one of his players' trousers and is rubbed against the ball. The ball-tampering player and his own team manager are promptly dispatched to the match referee. What the player has to say for himself, the chairman of selectors later admits, isn't "completely honest".

Sandpapergate live updates: Cummins hits out at Khawaja claims as 'complete and utter nonsense'

The player is duly excoriated and his punishment doubled on account of his lying. The press goes into overdrive. Career-ending sackings are called for but don't quite eventuate. And then, eventually, everyone moves on.

The player is not Cameron Bancroft, in case you haven't already guessed. It is Michael Atherton, about whom most of us probably hold far more positive views: a brave opening batter, a thoughtful and perceptive TV and newspaper analyst and something close to a conscience figure in the game, beyond reproach despite that regrettable interlude at Lord's in 1994.

Then-England captain Michael Atherton (right) was caught in his own ball-tampering firestorm during a South Africa tour in 1994. (Getty Images: PA Images/Adam Butler)

This raises questions about recent events that were not adequately answered in 2018, when Australia's tampering crisis exploded. Firstly, in these tumultuous, adversarial times, can we no longer hold multiple ideas in our heads at once?

Are we really not mature and reasonable enough to say that in the unending and sometimes bitter pursuit of the success Australians demand of them, our cricketers occasionally take things too far, just as Atherton did?

Are we really to put aside the plainly obvious truth that Sandpapergate was, in and of itself, a trifling matter for which a select few got stung with the compound interest on decades of accumulated grievances against entitled, poorly behaved Australian cricketers?

What is in Usman Khawaja's book Sabr and what did he actually say about Sandpapergate? Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

And are we really going to keep shooting the messenger? We might think Usman Khawaja naive, but in our heart of hearts, have we ever really believed that three batters were the only ones who knew about a minor cheating scheme that was of no direct personal benefit to them?

It is possible this entire affair now says far more about the Australian cricket public than it does our cricketers. It certainly says more about their bosses.

As was the case in 2018, the public expressions of dismay, both informed and not, speak of one positive: Australians care deeply about Test cricket and take it personally when they feel its honour is being sullied.

Equally, the defensiveness, the reflexive and faintly sinister demolition of Khawaja's character, and the "leave it in the past" mentality show that an unfortunately large cohort are in favour of administrators burying any form of dishonesty or wrongdoing by their own team, no matter the strength of the evidence in front of their eyes.

Usman Khawaja has faced a character assassination from parts of Australia after the release of his book earlier this week. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

It is precisely this dogma that got Australia in this mess in the first place: there is a line, but we decide where it is and whether or not we've crossed it. And when we do, we will bully into submission anyone who talks about it more honestly.

So many people have made this issue about themselves; perhaps you can permit me two personal anecdotes that illustrate broader points that have not been taken seriously enough.

In the first, I am, from memory, nine years old, down at the local cricket club, standing with other boys in a semicircle around our coach. He has in his hand a two-piece Red King cricket ball that has been battered so often against our cyclone fencing practice nets that it looks like roadkill. The coach is showing us what to do when a ball has degenerated beyond spit and polish treatment: pick the seam, gouge one side, hope for the best.

In the second, I'm in my mid-30s, working as a publisher but engaged in the unliterary task of searching the abrasives aisle of the local hardware store for the perfect piece of yellow sandpaper. It will be torn into small pieces and photographed to feature on the cover of Gideon Haigh's Sandpapergate book, Crossing the Line: How Australian Cricket Lost Its Way.

The roughing-up of a cricket ball via unconventional and illegal methods is commonplace in park cricket around Australia. (Supplied: Cricket NSW)

The first scenario was a point made with possibly unnecessary force this week by Stuart MacGill: everybody does it and always has (although perhaps not on the wall of the SCG dugout). Any club cricketer who says they are unfamiliar with at least some form of ball alteration is either an extremely disengaged teammate or a member of Pinocchio's Invitational XI.

As for the second, and putting aside the claim that Australian batsmen were using sandpaper on their bats — not beyond the realms of possibility, but behaviour that would be "rare" in both senses that cricketers use that word — it prompted a feeling that has never left me: "Someone in the Australian cricket team made this exact trip to Bunnings warehouse."

There were, in other words, both subconscious cultural factors and very obvious acts of premeditation at play in 2018 that always made the denials appear ludicrous.

Frankly, it is time that a lot of people grew up and acknowledged that a messy pile of accumulated facts are occasionally going to contradict each other, and that the truth is not as neat as a cricket scorecard. Some key points we should always bear in mind:

It is unlikely that Warner (left), Smith (centre left) and Bancroft (centre right) were the only players who knew the ball was being tampered with in South Africa. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

One: it is implausible that only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were aware the ball was being altered.

Two: many lies were, and since have been, told in service of Cricket Australia's process of "investigation", which put public relations priorities well ahead of the truth.

Three: having committed to a PR version of punishment, acting not in response to a case of ball tampering but to a public relations disaster, Cricket Australia was bound to hand out disproportionate penalties that have warped our rational sense of wrongdoing.

Four: the actual truth — or at least a version of it that did not insult our intelligence — was always bound to come out eventually. That it has occurred when some of the extremely well-remunerated players are still main characters should not mean it is buried again.

Mitchell Starc (centre) this week offered a strong rebuke to Khawaja's (right) allegations that the whole team knew of the sandpaper being brought into the field. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Five: Test cricketers are human beings, as prone to white lies and interpersonal dramas as the rest of us, with the added burden of intense scrutiny of their every move. The idea that any one of them would experience, process and recall certain events the same way as another is preposterous.

Six: It is equally preposterous to think every Australian player gets on with his teammates all the time, or that inevitable frictions are as dramatic as they have been made out to be. Australian Test stars of previous generations have, in books and post-career media work, detailed threatened (and actual) lawsuits against each other, exposure of infidelities, even death threats. Most of them have hugged it out in the end.

What many fans are left with, probably, is the similarly vague sense of anger and resentment — "This again? Really?" — that followed the original events. Cricket is a game for soul-searchers and its history is pockmarked with these moral eruptions.

Anger, in this case as in others before it, needs a target. The easiest one is Khawaja, because it is less practical and cathartic to direct it at faceless administrators. But make no mistake: back then, they absolutely bottled a situation that demanded level heads, and now they claim there is nothing else to see here.

Loading...

What would a level-headed reaction have looked like in 2018? That was the question faced by English chairman of selectors Ray Illingworth when he dealt with the Atherton affair.

To go with the media's lashings, Atherton was fined £2,000 — a proactive measure to ward off the suspension that was the preference of the Australian match referee, Peter Burge.

Years later, Illingworth pondered what a suspension would have meant for Atherton. "It could have finished him off as captain," he wrote in 2006. "[But] I don't think he would have been happy no matter the outcome."

"We were the first country to step in on the matter. Richie Benaud came up to me afterwards and said: 'Well done, you've handled it brilliantly.'"

It is something nobody would say of Cricket Australia.

World.title: Marsh dodges Sandpapergate questions in testy press conference exchange
World.content:
Australia's one-day captain, Mitch Marsh, has refused to address key aspects of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal as journalists peppered him with questions at a press conference.

Marsh, who was bowling when Cameron Bancroft was spotted hiding a piece of sandpaper in his pants during the 2018 series, spent most of the 12-minute press conference straight-batting questions about the infamous South Africa tour and Usman Khawaja's explosive allegations.

The very first question put to Marsh was: "Did you know that sandpaper was being used to tamper with cricket balls in South Africa?"

"Jeez, you hit a six off the first ball there, mate. Well done," Marsh replied.

Loading Instagram content

"I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I'm not here to share mine.

"I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us, and it's an important time for this one-day group.

"I really respect that Uzzy has told his story. He's written his book, and my focus is really on tomorrow."

Marsh was continually peppered with questions about why he was not willing to speak on the topic.

"I've personally moved on," he said.

Mitch Marsh says he has no ill feelings towards Usman Khawaja for the allegations made in his book. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"I respect that others probably haven't, but I have, and I hope that's respected.

"This is my choice to not go back there. Who knows? Maybe I'll write a book one day."

Marsh insisted he held no grudges against Khawaja.

"I respect Uzzy for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgement," Marsh said.

"Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on.

"It's really important that at some stage we do."

Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins, is set to front a press conference in Sydney tomorrow morning and has promised to answer "any and all media".

AAP

World.title: FA scrambles for Jordan alternative with Socceroos reluctant to travel
World.content:
Socceroos players remain unwilling to travel to Jordan as Football Australia (FA) scrambles for alternatives to playing an upcoming friendly in Amman.

But US Soccer's decision to withdraw its team from the under-17 World Cup in ‌Qatar over safety concerns is not expected to affect either the Socceroos or their Joeys counterparts.

The Socceroos and Joeys are both in camp in Doha ahead of their respective friendlies and World Cup campaigns.

Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The senior team is due to face Qatar on Saturday (AEDT) before travelling to Amman to face Jordan on November 18.

The latter is the issue, with PFA boss Beau Busch saying last week that Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

FA had been keen for the game in Jordan to proceed, but has said it was monitoring the security situation in the area.

The friendlies against Qatar and Jordan were arranged as preparations for January's Asian Cup, but the postponement of the tournament to December 2027 due to conflict in Saudi Arabia has decreased their significance.

Martin Kugeler has flown to Doha to find a solution. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar)

FA heavy hitters including chief executive Martin Kugeler and football director Heather Garriock flew to Doha this week, as did Busch and men's head of player relations Jon McKain.

Players are not expected to back down and agree to play in Jordan, likely leaving cancellation or relocation as the options.

One option is Australia remaining in Qatar and playing Jordan in Doha.

But that proposal is understood to have been met with some reluctance from both the Qatari and Jordanian football associations.

Jordan has already had to deal with Indonesia pulling out of a friendly this window.

Playing the Jordan game somewhere in southern Europe is another option, along with cancelling or postponing the game altogether.

Coach Tony Popovic, due to speak to media in his pre-match press conference on Thursday night, has indicated no players would be blacklisted from future selection if they withdrew from his squad for security reasons.

Elsewhere, in ‌a letter sent to players, US Soccer said it was cancelling its team's pre-tournament camp and its participation in the under-17 World Cup "in light of current circumstances".

US Soccer cited US State Department's Level 3 travel advisory for Qatar and related ‌directives for ‌embassy ⁠staff and families.

But the Joeys are not expected to follow the US in withdrawing from the under-17 tournament in Qatar, while the Socceroos are understood not to have issues with being in Qatar.

AAP

World.title: Kiwi duo Ponga and Waaka claim Golden Boot awards after stunning seasons
World.content:
New Zealand duo Kalyn Ponga and Stacey Waaka have been named the men's and women's Golden Boot winners after outstanding individual seasons at their respective clubs.

Ponga scored six tries as he led Newcastle to the NRL grand final before scoring two further tries for the Kiwis at the Rugby League World Cup despite suffering a broken arm.

Waaka, a cross-code star, scored nine tries for the Warriors in just 10 NRLW appearances and added nine tries in four World Cup appearances.

Both players will be in action for New Zealand's men's and women's sides in their respective World Cup finals this weekend as they take on Australia.

Ponga is New Zealand's eighth men's Golden Boot winner, joining Hugh McGahan, Stacey Jones, Benji Marshall, Shaun Johnson, Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, Joseph Manu and James Fisher-Harris.

Waaka is the third New Zealand player to win the women's award, joining Raecene McGregor and Georgia Hale.

Ponga edged out his Cup final counterpart Reece Walsh, Samoa powerhouse Francis Manulelua, Tonga centre Robert Toia and Kiwi centre Casey McLean who were all shortlisted for the men's award.

The Wheelchair golden boot was taken out by England's Rob Hawkins ahead of Friday night's final in Wollongong between England and France.

World.title: Addo-Carr free to leave Eels as club rejects extension opportunity
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr is free to leave Parramatta immediately after the Eels advised the former Test winger the club would not offer him a contract extension beyond 2027.

After a series of bizarre twists and turns, the Eels have decided Addo-Carr is not wanted after next season and he can start hunting for a new NRL club.

The development comes despite the NRL integrity unit clearing the 31-year-old to return to Parramatta after failing a roadside random drugs test in October.

The ex-NSW State of Origin and Kangaroos star received an unexpected lifeline when his B sample came back negative earlier this month.

"The Parramatta Eels would like to provide an update regarding Josh Addo-Carr following a driving incident in September," an Eels statement read on Thursday.

"After reviewing all relevant information, including the negative result of the B sample, the club has cleared Josh in relation to the issues raised following the incident.

"The NRL has also confirmed it will not be taking any further action, and the club now considers the matter closed.

"Separately, the club has informed Josh and his management that it will not be seeking to extend his current contract beyond the end of the 2027 season."

The Eels will keep the door ajar for Addo-Carr to see out his 2027 contract, but will not stand in his way if he secures a new contract with a rival club.

The 31-year-old is due back at pre-season training with the Eels next week, as his management looks to secure the flyer a future elsewhere.

AAP

Tech.title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
Tech.content:
Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.”

Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.”

Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8, and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

Tech.title: ‘It’s a mistake’: reactions from tech leaders on Jensen Huang’s resignation
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report. The situation surrounding Huang has unfolded quickly, with The New York Times only reporting on Friday that Huang and the suspected spy were “close” before other dominoes started to fall, leading to a swift fall from grace for one of the biggest names in technology. (Hours after Huang’s resignation was announced, Reuters reported that he also had an “intimate relationship” with another Nvidia employee.)

Prominent voices in technology have come out in support of Huang, with some calling the resignation a “waste” and a sad day for “all humanity.” The narrative among those leaders on X, at least, is that Huang’s resignation was rushed — perhaps an overreaction to salacious news stories about his personal life. Some others have had a more neutral reaction, commenting more on Huang’s achievements at the company’s helm. You can see a collection of those responses below.

President Donald Trump

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”, Trump said on Truth Social.

Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO

Elon Musk said in a reply to an X user that it would “be an honor” to hire Huang. He also replied to a post that said “You’d think we’d have learned from Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick that one does not just simply replace the founder…” by saying “True words.”

Tim Sweeney, Epic Games CEO

Sweeney said that today is “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction.”

Ahead of Huang’s resignation, Sweeney posted about how Huang “saved” a GDC 2015 presentation by dropping off a graphics card and said that “The dude truly is the visionary driver of the future of tech from the gaming GPU era to CUDA to AI supercomputers.”

Palmer Luckey, Anduril founder

“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said last night, before Huang’s resignation was announced.

Matt Mullenweg, Automattic co-founder and CEO

Mullenweg reposted an X post that followed his brief September ouster as CEO: “Founder advice: If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders.” He said, “Just putting this back out there, for no reason whatsoever.”

David Heinemeier Hansson, 37signals CTO and creator of the Omarchy Linux distribution

“What a waste,” Hansson said this morning, replying to his own post from hours before: “NVIDIA would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board. Have some proportionality.”

Clément Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face (which Nvidia recently acquired for almost $13 billion)

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened,” Delangue said. “It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!

Changpeng Zhao, former Binance CEO

“It’s a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign,” Zhao said.

Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw creator and OpenAI employee

“If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” Steinberger said. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” (“I agree,” replied Sweeney.)

Aravind Srinivas, Perplexity co-founder and CEO

Srinivas thanked Huang for “33 years of bold leadership” in a post this morning. “You built a small startup into America’s most valuable company, with relentless improvement. Your grit and perseverance should always be remembered. Your personal generosity with time and advice to founders like me has secured a bright future for America and AI.”

Jason Calacanis, All-In Podcast host

Calacanis reposted Trump’s post, tagging Tim Cook and telling him to “Keep the seat warm” for Huang while “the investigation is sorted out” and saying that “America needs you Mr. Cook.” Last night, he also said that Nvidia shareholders should “decide Jensen’s fate after the investigation is complete — not the press or online mobs.”

Lex Fridman, Lex Fridman Podcast host

In a post talking about how he has seen Huang show “kindness, humility, care to everyone around him,” Fridman said that “I’m in shock frankly at all of this, including the mass hysteria around it. I love America, and I think NVIDIA letting Jensen go is terrible for America. I stand with Jensen.”

Tech.title: Here are the 25 original Xbox games you can now play on PC
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For the 25th anniversary of Xbox, Microsoft is beginning to make good on its paid “next-gen game preservation” promise. Starting today, you can play 25 different original Xbox games on your Windows PC, as long as you have (or are willing to pay) for digital copies.

In July, Microsoft originally launched the idea with just four Xbox games, so 25 is progress, and Microsoft says all these games are now playable with keyboard and mouse.

Plus, Microsoft says it’s adding achievements to original Xbox games for the first time, starting with four games: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and its sequel, Blinx: The Time Sweeper, and Conker: Live and Reloaded. You can unlock achievements playing them on Xbox One and Xbox Series consoles as well, after a system update. More games should get them in future.

Here’s the full list of Xbox on PC games, with the 21 new additions in bold:

Armed and Dangerous

Blinx: The Time Sweeper

Conker: Live and Reloaded

Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge

Disney’s Chicken Little

The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind

Fuzion Frenzy

Grabbed by the Ghoulies

Indiana Jones and the Emperor’s Tomb

Red Faction II

Secret Weapons Over Normandy

Star Wars Battlefront

Star Wars Battlefront II

Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith

Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy

Star Wars Jedi Knight II Jedi Outcast

Star Wars: Jedi Starfighter

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II – The Sith Lords

Star Wars: Republic Commando

Star Wars: Starfighter – Special Edition

Star Wars: The Clone Wars

Thrillville

TimeSplitters 2

TimeSplitters: Future Perfect

Yes, that’s a lot of Star Wars games, most of which already have a PC version, and few games that were exclusive to Xbox at the time. (But many of those Star Wars games were excellent.)

You also won’t be able to use an original Xbox disc to play these games, I’m afraid, as original Xbox (and Xbox 360) discs aren’t part of Microsoft’s disc-to-digital program; they predate the unique serial number that Microsoft embedded into Xbox One discs. In case you’re wondering, Xbox on PC backward compatibility appears to be powered by an emulator.

Also, most of the new games aren’t currently included with Xbox Game Pass, according to Microsoft; just Blinx, Conker, Crimson Skies, Fusion Frenzy, Morrowind, and Grabbed by the Ghoulies.

Tech.title: Meet the people who want peptides to be made in America
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. We’ll be taking a break next week and will be back on November 25th. Opt in for Optimizer here.

The SS Jeremiah O’Brien is a World War II Liberty ship. The hulking vessel was built in 56 days. It made 11 trips to Normandy, France, to supply the Allied powers in the fight against German U-boats. Last week, it was the site of a black-tie peptide party thrown by a trio of Gen Z venture capitalists.

Roughly 150 people attended the event, where four types of peptide samples were provided to guests — no injections. One was a topical cream with GHK-Cu, while the other three were dissolvable sublingual strips from peptide startup Afterglow. GHK-Cu is a popular skincare ingredient, but it’s unclear how well sublingual peptide strips work. The topic of the night wasn’t just the state of peptides. The venue was a deliberate reference to American industrial prowess — and why the pharmaceutical supply chain ought to be centered in the United States.

The timing couldn’t have been more pointed.

Sourcing is one of the biggest question marks with gray-market peptides — something the US Department of Health and Human Services is trying to address with its recent interim policy decision allowing certain unapproved peptides for compounding.

The decision is a controversial one. FDA career scientists haven’t endorsed it, though to the average person it might seem like they have. In fact, at a public hearing in July, FDA scientists categorically stated that there wasn’t enough evidence proving safety or efficacy for the experimental peptides in question. Some industry experts have cautioned that the HHS’s decision threatens the current clinical trial framework. By circumventing gold-standard clinical trials, it arguably allows telehealth providers and compounding pharmacies to bypass the approval process and create a parallel, dubiously regulated market.

But for the party’s organizers Roxana Grunenwald, Yuva Krishnapillai, and Elia Ahmadi — all three are from Haus Fund, a biotech accelerator — this was an opportunity to make the case for American peptides. Hence the party on a wartime cargo ship, where guests left with stickers and hats emblazoned with “My Peptides Are Made in America.”

Haus Fund’s Gen Z VCs talk “Biological Dynamism.” Photo: Haus Fund

Listening to the three speak, they wouldn’t strike you as typical hooah patriots or MAHA activists — though there’s some overlap in their talking points. They’re venture capitalists promoting a certain viewpoint that’s trending in Silicon Valley right now. But it’s not just them making this argument. Hims & Hers — one of the most recognizable telehealth brands right now — is also hopping on the American peptide bandwagon.

The push for American manufacturing is a thorny one. Last year, President Donald Trump’s tariff policies also reignited the American manufacturing argument, though the reality is it’s difficult to return to “made in America” after decades spent shaping the country into a services-based economy.

Pharmaceuticals have also globalized. According to the US Pharmacopeia, 51 percent of all US prescription active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) comes from India and the European Union. China accounts for 10 percent. But when it comes to gray-market peptides, there’s a reason they’re commonly referred to as “Chinese peptides.” The vast majority of these research chemicals sold online come from Chinese manufacturers.

“Right now, Americans are buying consumer peptides from gray-market sellers in China. And that concerns me because American consumers have little recourse if something goes wrong,” Ahmadi said in response to a panel question. “This is not a blanket criticism of China. This is not a criticism of Chinese people. America needs to be able to make its own medicines.”

“I think this is a really good first step in solving the gray market problem,” Krishnapillai tells me, referring to the HHS’s interim decision. While building industrial infrastructure is a lengthy, complicated, and expensive process, he argues that this decision opens the door for compounding pharmacies to build a supply chain that adheres to US consumer safety laws. That in turn could give the FDA more insight into how to more effectively regulate the market. “The FDA [will be] able to see from a bird’s-eye view a lot more clarity, which will allow for structure to be built out and eventually a new path to API classification,” he adds.

“We’re taking the stance that if people will be purchasing these peptides and taking them, sometimes even injecting, we want them to be American peptides,” adds Grunenwald. “We want them to be both compounded, produced, and verified on American soil.”

“The hardware industry — semiconductors, the compute industry, electronics — have all recognized that the reliance on China for critical minerals is a huge issue. That’s very clear. The bio industry has not yet had that same pushback and the same epiphany about our reliance on Chinese APIs. We aim to bring this onshore. It’ll take a lot of money and a lot of time, but it’s not impossible,” says Grunenwald.

For Ahmadi, onshoring peptides back to America is also a matter of regulatory consistency.

“That made-in-America stamp is really only the beginning,” he says. “If we don’t have our own domestic production, we won’t be able to enforce our own regulations. Our markets are always going to be flooded by foreign imports and we won’t be able to have accountability to American consumers. So, we see this as the first step in a larger conversation to have America set the global standard for quality and safety in this new space.”

Broadly speaking, these points have some merit. Several gray-market peptide users I’ve spoken with for an upcoming story stated that the mere act of importing “research drugs” and worrying about customs was a significant source of anxiety. That said, cost is another major reason why my sources tell me they opted to seek Chinese suppliers. It’s too soon to tell, but American-made peptides will likely be more expensive. That’s because an end-to-end US supply chain for these drugs is no easy feat.

Even so, for some, that extra expense is worth it if it means signaling a higher-quality product.

“We purchased an API manufacturing facility in California recently … Our intention is to leverage that capability to provide US-made API, and as a result, US-made product through the whole supply chain,” says Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer at Hims & Hers. The company purchased the facility last year, though it does partner with other companies globally to deliver compounded medications outside the US.

Hims is launching Peptide Plus just as they purchased a new California manufacturing facility.

But in this particular case, Vinjamoori is also specifically referring to Peptides Plus, a forthcoming service from Hims & Hers announced in the wake of the HHS interim policy. In a blog announcing Peptides Plus, Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum writes that the company “spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own U.S.-based peptide manufacturing facility.” At launch, the company plans to provide access to “Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable.” Notably, some of these substances, like vitamin B12 and NAD+, aren’t peptides at all. Meanwhile, sermorelin and glutathione are already legal. All of these, with the exception of BPC-157 and TB-500, are currently available through legal pathways.

“I think it’s important not just to be able to say, ‘Oh, this is US made,’ but because it gives us direct oversight into the whole process,” says Vinjamoori, who says that he had prescribed peptides to patients in the past before the Biden administration moved certain research peptides to the no-compounding list.

“Even then, there was inconsistency between compounding pharmacies. Everyone knew this,” he says, noting that doctors would individually recommend pharmacies based on what they were prescribing. “That to me, is still not ideal. That’s why we really felt it was worth making this investment — and to be clear, this is not easy.”

When asked about how this might affect Peptide Plus pricing, Vinjamoori demurred, stating that the company would have more to share in “due time.”

There are yet many unknowns with regard to the HHS decision and how it’ll impact the peptide economy at large. The decision is most notably an interim policy. It’s not necessarily a permanent or lasting change. It was also made before the midterm elections, so who can say how the policy winds will shift concerning tariffs and whether the zeal for “made in America” will fizzle as a result.

But for now, it’s more than likely that you’ll start seeing some vendors touting that their peptides are proudly made in America. It’s entirely possible that they might imply that makes their product “safer.” That might be true with regard to sourcing and, to a degree, accountability. But it’s not the whole story. After all, in peptide America, sourcing is only part of the problem.

Tech.title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
Tech.content:
Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.

Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.

The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.

“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog.

Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier.

“I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.”

Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades.

“This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.”

Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.”

“Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge. “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’”

“Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.”

The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics. While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place.

Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.”

Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.
